MR. MATTE-ALLEGED INACCURATE ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS ON LOCAL INITIATIVES PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleagues and I have repeatedly, over the past few weeks, sought clarification of the confusion related to the Local Initiatives Program.
The replies to my oral questions seem to be absolutely contradictory to facts and they mislead the House.
When questioned by the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Godin) on February 28 last, the parliamentary secretary stated that on February 25 there were still $4,000,000 to distribute. The Minister of Labour, on March 2, gave a vague reply to a question on the same subject posed by my colleague from Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert).
As for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), he replied that he would take under advisement the questions put by the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Latulippe) and myself as to the possibility of increasing or transferring funds. Nothing further was done about that.
Nor have I been able, in spite of several questions, to determine when funds available for Quebec were used up.
Mr. Speaker, such a procedure is a direct infringement on our rights and privileges as representatives of the people.
It is inacceptable that we should be unable to give accurate information to some 700 Quebec municipalities which have been misinformed and frustrated, and all the more since the statements of the Quebec minister in charge contradict allegations of officials of the Department of Manpower and Immigration.
We therefore demand an official statement from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) or the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Mackasey) in this connection.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: PRINCE RUPERT-INCLUSION AS NATIONAL HARBOURS BOARD PORT-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce to the House that the port of Prince Rupert will become the tenth National Harbours Board port.

subtopic: PRINCE RUPERT-INCLUSION AS NATIONAL HARBOURS BOARD PORT-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: PRINCE RUPERT-INCLUSION AS NATIONAL HARBOURS BOARD PORT-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Two recommendations to the Governor in Council that will have an important bearing on the future of Prince Rupert have been accepted. One recommendation extends the limits of Prince Rupert harbour and transfers the administration, management and control of the harbour to the National Harbours Board. The other confirms the acceptance by Canada of the transfer by the province of British Columbia of the administration, control and benefit of certain Crown lands at Prince Rupert for the purpose of operating a national harbour.
I am looking forward to inviting representatives of the community to serve as members of the Port of Prince Rupert Authority, which will be created at the earliest possible opportunity.
I will also ask the National Harbours Board to invite proposals that will lead to the establishment of a major modern grain transshipment facility at Prince Rupert. This is in anticipation of a larger proportion of grain shipments to China and Russia and the Pacific rim countries being directed over the northern route, thus relieving congestion in the Fraser River canyon and elsewhere.
The National Harbours Board will also undertake studies related to its own possible involvement in such facilities. I want to emphasize that the federal government is seeking to further the development of the port of Prince Rupert in conjunction with the development of other ports, such as the port of Vancouver. The objective is to provide both greater capacity and greater flexibility, and to improve access to the Pacific.
1072

March 23, 1972
Prince Rupert Harbour
The National Harbours Board will continue to support and pursue other initiatives that anticipate the development of bulk handling and general cargo facilities in the port of Prince Rupert. Provision has been made in the board's 1972-73 estimates for a $5 million expenditure at this port.
I think the House will also be interested in knowing that the National Harbours Board has opened a business office in Winnipeg to serve western Canadian requirements. The growth in grain, bulk commodity and general cargo movements is such that full co-ordination of transportation and transshipment facilities is essential. It is anticipated that the new office will contribute to the establishing of more efficient traffic flows through the ports of Vancouver, Prince Rupert, Churchill and Thunder Bay.

subtopic: PRINCE RUPERT-INCLUSION AS NATIONAL HARBOURS BOARD PORT-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the House welcome this announcement, but we wonder why it has taken so long-

subtopic: PRINCE RUPERT-INCLUSION AS NATIONAL HARBOURS BOARD PORT-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: PRINCE RUPERT-INCLUSION AS NATIONAL HARBOURS BOARD PORT-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
-to recognize Prince Rupert. We are fully aware that the Prime Minister made a trip to the Pacific rim countries some years ago and more or less suggested that trade should pick up with that area. Prince Rupert is far closer to Japan and China than is Vancouver and therefore it is the natural port from which to ship to those countries.
We will reserve our final judgment on the government and the expenditure until we see how the government goes about it. A few years ago funds were allotted to the department for the development of the port of Vancouver under the National Harbours Board, but the board did not use all of the allotted moneys for that port. Whether the $5 million for Prince Rupert will be spent in the right manner is hard to determine at this time. There are only two wharves at Prince Rupert, only one of which handles grain. Also-, there is the so-called surge problem at the port. We hope that some money will be allocated to correct this problem, and we certainly hope that the grain handling facilities will be enlarged.
The minister suggests that bulk handling and general cargo facilities should be improved. We certainly agree they should be because ships must be able to come into Prince Rupert with a cargo and also leave the port with a cargo. Part of the difficulty has been in getting ships with cargoes to come to Prince Rupert. Access by rail to Edmonton and the northern parts of the prairie region is far shorter from Prince Rupert and therefore we have always looked upon Prince Rupert as a valuable port which should be developed.
We welcome this initial step by the government and we will watch the expenditures carefully to make certain that this port proves to be the tremendous asset it could be, particularly to the grain economy in the northern parts of the Prairies as well as the whole prairie region.

subtopic: PRINCE RUPERT-INCLUSION AS NATIONAL HARBOURS BOARD PORT-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will refrain from mentioning the difficulties which we had in trying to get the grain storage facilities at Prince Rupert doubled between 1958 and 1962.

subtopic: PRINCE RUPERT-INCLUSION AS NATIONAL HARBOURS BOARD PORT-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: PRINCE RUPERT-INCLUSION AS NATIONAL HARBOURS BOARD PORT-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
We have been awaiting this announcement not just for months, as might appear to be the case, but ever since 1919 when the late Mackenzie King visited Prince Rupert and made these commitments. Seriously, Mr. Speaker, this matter has been in the minds of everybody in Prince Rupert and the surrounding area for a long period of time, and certainly this is a welcome announcement on the part of the minister. We look forward to the establishment of the port authority itself, the involvement of the National Harbours Board, and the development of the port for obvious reasons that are clear to everyone, namely, shipments in and out of the port of Prince Rupert, particularly of grain, thus helping to relieve the pressure on other ports and other parts of the country.
Up until now Mr. Bill Raithie, a member for the National Harbours Board, has acted as liaison between the federal government and the provincial government with respect to the transfer of land. I would hope, with all respect to Mr. Raithie, that he would have a minimum of involvement in whatever happens in the city of Prince Rupert from the National Harbours Board point of view. He is chairman of the Vancouver Port Authority, and I believe that his interests are mainly directed there and that he should not have too much involvement with Prince Rupert for that reason.
In the establishment of the Port of Prince Rupert authority I hope the minister would go beyond the boundaries of the city and include persons from the organized community of Port Edward.
I do not know what the minister means by a major, modern grain transshipment facility at Prince Rupert. At the present time there is a storage capacity there of 2\ million bushels, or a little less. I would suggest that he, the National Harbours Board, or whoever is going to do this work, should be thinking at least in terms of a storage capacity of 10 million bushels and the installation of a tipple system so that boxcars can move in loaded with clearn grain and be unloaded rapidly with a minimum of difficulty, thus making maximum use of the port.
This will also mean, I hope, increased use of the Canadian National facilities running in and out of the port of Prince Rupert. If that is the case-in fact, even without increased use of Canadian National facilities-I think that Canadian National, in conjunction with the province of British Columbia if they can work out an agreement or by itself if they cannot, should move into the installation of snowsheds along the lower reaches of the Skeena River. At this time of year and earlier in the winter there are periods of a week, ten days and sometimes up to two weeks when there is no rail movement in and out of that area because of snow slides. Snowsheds would help to alleviate that problem.
I would not like to see this port when it is developed, used simply as an exit port for raw materials or nearly raw materials. The more we continue to export raw materials out of the nation the more we export jobs with them and the more we provide jobs to people in manufacturing industries in other countries. I would rather see us expand our own manufacturing industries, process raw

March 23, 1972

materials into useable goods, and export useable goods rather then export our natural wealth in the form of raw materials.
I am sure the people of Prince Rupert would endorse the concepts I am now expressing and would want me to express their appreciation to the minister for his announcement. We look forward to further action in the future.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF RETENTION OF CANADIAN FORCES BASE AT SUMMERSIDE IN PRESENT ROLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to be my day for making announcements. Hon. members will recall that in 1969 it was announced by the government that the Canadian Forces Base at Summerside, Prince Edward Island, was having its life extended as a military base to the end of 1973 in order to provide time during which it might be determined whether alternative uses could be found for the base. This effort has been going on for quite some time, and I think it is generally known that it has not been possible to obtain enough in the way of alternative uses to take the place of the base. So, as one who worked on that committee, and on behalf of my colleague, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Benson), I wish to inform the House that Canadian Forces Base Summerside, Prince Edward Island, will continue in its present operational role.
It will be recalled that Canadian Forces Base Summer-side was one of several defence bases that were recommended for closure under an armed forces base consolidation plan that was worked out some years ago. In December, 1969, an extension of its operation was granted until April of this year to permit a study of the economic impact that closure would have on the local community and the province. A thorough investigation of the alternatives has clearly demonstrated that the base should be confirmed in its present role.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF RETENTION OF CANADIAN FORCES BASE AT SUMMERSIDE IN PRESENT ROLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the announcement made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) on behalf of his colleague the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Benson) is most welcome. I especially appreciate it as the base to which he refers is in my constituency. I am delighted that this decision has been made not only because of the high operational quality that has been maintained there from a defence point of view, the high morale that has existed and the higher than average level of competency that has been demonstrated by the personnel but because, and in some ways more important, this base is a very important economic factor in the life of Prince Edward Island and in the future of the town of Summerside. On all these scores the announcement is indeed very welcome not only for its own value but also because it removes the doubt which clouded the economic future of that area since the suggestion was first made that the base might not continue.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: STATEMENT BY SECRETARY OF STATE ON 1972 OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to give a progress report to the House on the response of young people to this year's Opportunities for Youth program.
On January 13, I announced that the budget for the 1972 program was $33,978,000 and that this money would fund jobs and activities for about 29,000 young men and women. Another 1,860 non-paying activities will also be created by the program. At the same time, I advised that the deadline for project applications was midnight, March 8. In other words, Mr. Speaker, applicants had almost two months to prepare their submissions. They were advised and helped in filling their application forms by 75 program field officers who were deployed across the country meeting young people at high schools, on college and university campuses, and conferring with municipal authorities and representatives of various public organizations.
Program officers and officials of the department assured that there was an adequate supply of application forms. Some 200,000 English and 100,000 French forms were available from various government outlets and from program workers. The program was extensively promoted in the print and broadcasting media.
As we anticipated, the younger generation's interest in the program has remained at a high level. Once again, they have shown their resourcefulness by the quality and variety of their proposals.
Canadian youth in all parts of the country submitted some 19,102 projects to the Opportunities for Youth Program head-quarters here in Ottawa. These applications are now being coded and processed. The spread of projects by region is as follows: Atlantic provinces, 3,189 or 17 per cent; Quebec, 6,688 or 35 per cent; Ontario, 4,046 or 21 per cent; Prairie provinces, 2,912 or 15 per cent; British Columbia, 2,104 or 11 per cent, and national, 173 or roughly one per cent. Project proposals average $11,949 each and would include an average of 10 participants. This is close to what program planners consider the ideal project size which should cost between $10,000 and $15,000 and employ between eight and 12 people.
In my January 13 press conference I said that we hoped to be able to put more stress on assisting students from disadvantaged environments. I think that with the very strong response we have received from the Atlantic provinces, Quebec and the rural sections of the Prairie provinces-60 per cent of the prairie applications came from rural areas-with this kind of response, I repeat, it should
1074

March 23, 1972
Opportunities for Youth Program
be easier to meet the objective of putting funds where they are needed most.
A special effort was also made this year to enhance the participation of women in projects. To date, 40 per cent of jobs proposed have been for women. Present analysis also indicates that 30 per cent of would-be participants are secondary or high school students, 63 per cent are postsecondary and seven per cent are non-students.

The largest groups of proposed projects involve recreational activities, 25 per cent, and social services, 20 per cent. Other estimates of projects are cultural, 16 per cent; environmental, 14 per cent; research, 11 per cent; information, 11 per cent, and miscellaneous, 2 per cent.
We are of course pleased by the strong response that the program has received in its second year. This response shows that the government was right when it decided to increase the program's budget by about $10 million this year. These additional resources should allow us to fund about 3,000 projects and participants should, on the whole, earn somewhat more than they received on the average last year. In other words, we foresee an average allocation of about $1,100 this year per participant compared with $900 last year. Unfortunately, many worthwhile projects will be rejected. But it was never intended that this program should be a total answer to summer employment for students. As in the past, a very large proportion of employment will be supplied by the private sector of the economy. And of course Opportunities for Youth is not the only federal program designed to promote useful summer activities and employment. In addition to our own department's efforts to support about 100 hostels across the country and other programs to promote travel and exchanges of young people, special efforts are being made by the Public Service Commission, the Department of National Defence, the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Department of Manpower to encourage student activities and employment under the general heading of Summer '72 programs. The over-all expenditure for the Summer '72 effort will be in the order of $85 million.
I would like now to say a word about the schedule for processing the applications received by the Opportunities for Youth program administration. All provincial governments have been consulted on their regional priorities and their views will be taken into account during the selection process. Officers of the department for which I am responsible and a staff of over 230 at the program's headquarters will participate in the selection. Processing will be computerized and selection will be based on such factors as conformity to the program's criteria, the numbers >i jobs per project, the employment needs of participants and the ratio between male and female participants, geographical distribution, recommendations from people in the community, specialist consultants, provincial priorities and the budgets allocated by region and sub-region.
It is expected that public announcements of accepted projects will be made from April 17 to 27. Each group of participants will be advised by letter of the approval of their projects. Throughout the summer, 100 field officers will be posted in the various regions to provide support

for the project workers, maintain contact with other community groups and offer resource assistance to projects.
I would ask applicants to bear with us while each submission is studied. We are aware that young people are anxious to know the results. First decisions should be announced by April 17. Groups are requested not to expect answers before that date.

maintopic: STATEMENT BY SECRETARY OF STATE ON 1972 OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are grateful for the minister's statement, particularly with regard to the progress report on this year's Opportunities for Youth program. There is no doubt that the Opportunities for Youth program both last year and this year is enjoying tremendous popularity with the young people of this country.

maintopic: STATEMENT BY SECRETARY OF STATE ON 1972 OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: STATEMENT BY SECRETARY OF STATE ON 1972 OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM
speechtext: The obvious rate of submissions, close to 20,000, is indication enough of the popularity of the program. It also indicates, and this was not mentioned in the minister's statement, the tremendous need of young people for employment this year.

maintopic: STATEMENT BY SECRETARY OF STATE ON 1972 OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM
speechtext: Oh, oh!

maintopic: STATEMENT BY SECRETARY OF STATE ON 1972 OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM
speechtext:
I find it passing strange that the minister would even dare comment on the employment possibilities of Opportunities for Youth without at once acknowledging the tremendous need and growing gap in terms of jobs for students and other young people during this present year. The minister talked about the possibility of employment this summer for approximately 30,000 young people under Opportunities for Youth; yet we know the summer labour force is going to increase by some 100,000 this year to a total of approximately 1,300,000. I see no acknowledgement in the minister's statement in this regard.
While I think all hon. members and many Canadians will rejoice in the opportunities that young people will have to develop their talents and skills creatively under Opportunities for Youth, we must not let this divert us from a basic concern about the need for employment by young people during this present year. We know only too well that during the past two years the rate of unemployment for those in the 14 to 24 age group has been running at more than twice the national level. This is simply not an acceptable figure for a modern country like Canada. Just the other day, a York University sociologist said:
Inadequate federal economic policy theories have given Canada the highest rate of youth unemployment in the industrialized western world-
That sociologist is not a particular friend of members on this side of the House. He was the chairman of the government's own committee on youth, Mr. David Hunter. It is well past time that this government acknowledged, if its total answer to the swelling ranks of unemployed youth is one program or a series of travelling opportunities, that this is not sufficient to meet the needs of this country. We ask, what answers and what action is the government prepared to put forward?
March 23, 1972

In his statement the minister was limited to saying: "Unfortunately many worth-while projects will be rejected. But it was never intended that this program should be a total answer to summer employment for students." That understatement is the masterpiece of the minister's career because it acknowledges the almost total failure of this government to realize what its basic responsibilities are with regard to youth and their importance to this country.
It is near the end of March and we are talking about a progress report on this year's Opportunities for Youth program. We were told last fall we would have a thoroughgoing evaluation of last summer's activities which would give us some clear idea as to the strategy and goals for this year's program. Where is that report? We got a gloss of it in December. We were again told in December that we would have the report shortly. We have been left to read in the usual fashion what the government is up to, through leaked reports in the daily press which tell us that the goals of meeting the youth unemployment crisis are being failed by this government.
There is a cqmplete lack of recognition and co-ordination. Only yesterday afternoon I sought the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion in these terms:
That the Secretary of State immediately consult with business and industry in order to develop a concerted approach to the imminent crisis in youth unemployment.
Unfortunately, some hon. members saw fit not to consent.
We have heard that somewhere in the minister's vast department some industrial referral centre is trying to deal with the five out of six projects that will not be accepted under the Opportunities for Youth; yet we have heard no specific mention or acknowledgement of this program. Basically, we are getting non-answers from an overworked minister with regard to the youth unemployment crisis. It seems to me at least that this minister is just not capable any longer of handling this tremendously important problem. It is time the government acknowledged that it has a basic responsibility to co-ordinate not only its own activities, but to suggest and allow for coordination of activities in other levels of government and in the private sector.
In the statement today we were not even told about the subjective parts of the selection process. Will there be any kind of negotiation as there was last year with regard to project submissions? What will be the criteria in subjective selection of projects? Will the final answer be that five out of six project groups will receive a form letter, as was the case last year, with reasons that are not clear as to why their project is not acceptable? That kind of answer is unacceptable to the members of this House and the people of this country.

maintopic: STATEMENT BY SECRETARY OF STATE ON 1972 OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all of us on this side of the House are getting tired of the government periodically and triumphantly trotting out temporary measures to deal with our now chronic problem of massive unemployment in this country. Opportunities for Youth, while it contains the germ of a good idea, that of providing young people with opportunities to conceive, plan and execute projects which they believe are interesting, challenging and socially worth while, is in the end
Opportunities for Youth Program simply another patch like the Local Initiatives Program on a system based on a dying, decaying economic philosophy.
These programs do not go even a small part of the way toward meeting the real needs of this country and its people, young or old. This country needs a government dedicated to the creation of full employment. Only full employment will provide real opportunities for youth, real opportunities for young adults, real opportunities for the middle-aged, real opportunities for the elderly, and avoid programs which are essentially government subsidies to an already, for the most part, privileged group. Opportunities for Youth is essentially a middle-class program for middle-class youth, an attempt to buy off an extremely able, highly articulate segment of our society who know, when discontented, how to apply pressure so it hurts.

maintopic: STATEMENT BY SECRETARY OF STATE ON 1972 OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: STATEMENT BY SECRETARY OF STATE ON 1972 OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM
speechtext:
It is this group that the government is attempting to buy off with Opportunities for Youth; it is attempting to buy them off and divert their attention from correcting the real social ills to which they would otherwise be devoting their attention.
I am fed up to the back teeth with middle-class programs for middle-class kids when there are no corresponding programs for the other 85 per cent of the population. Leaving aside other age groups, what does this program do for the 75 per cent of the young people who are not in universities or community colleges?
Where did the minister say his 75 field workers spent their time? Was it among the 70 per cent of the young people who might have some difficulty in setting down their ideas for worth-while projects in a manner which would impress someone sitting behind a desk in Ottawa evaluating those submissions? No. The minister told us with evident pride that the field workers spent their time "meeting young people at high schools, on college and university campuses and conferring with municipal officials and representatives of various public organizations".
I ask hon. members, are these the people who need assistance in making preparations? They are already where they are because they have demonstrated some facility in communication. When is this government going to do something really meaningful to assist the disadvantaged in this country? I have given up hope.
The ultimate perversion is that some former employees of the Opportunities for Youth program of last year set themselves up in business writing submissions for people who wish to apply this year. As one former employee of Opportunities for Youth said:
We are producing a generation of professional grants-men, kids from universities with long training in how to deal with this era of public grant giving.
I have nothing at all against doing something for college and university students-far from it-but not to the exclusion of everyone else and not with a program which does not even meet the needs of that group of society. Last year I was willing to put up with mistakes in the conception and execution of Opportunities for Youth because it was a new program, all too rapidly thrown together. This year I am not, not after a year's experience and certainly not

March 23, 1972
Opportunities for Youth Program after the promised evaluations of last year's program turned out to be cooked information and the independent evaluation has either been stolen or lost. If I sound churlish, Mr. Speaker, it is because I am disappointed, and I make no bones about it.

maintopic: STATEMENT BY SECRETARY OF STATE ON 1972 OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Secertary of State (Mr. Pelletier) for being kind enough to forward a copy of his statement to us.
As he indicated, the record number of 19,000 projects submitted by student groups is proof enough that young Canadians are interested in participating in Canadian community life.
On many occasions in this House, I emphasized this wish for participation on the part of our young people, who are receptive and ready to contribute their full share to the Canadian community.
The Opportunities for Youth program will certainly be helpful to a great number of them. The only hitch is that it will be impossible to accept all the projects submitted.
I hope that the group in charge of assessing and examining the projects will be objective in the selection, so that last year's errors are not repeated.
During the past few weeks, I have had a look at some of the projects submitted from my constituency. I am quite impressed with their originality and seriousness of design. This is why I should be disappointed if some serious projects were rejected. The project screening group has an important task to perform and I hope that it will approach it very earnestly.
I thank the minister for submitting this first report to the House and I invite him once more to keep us informed in this respect.

At the end of January, 1972, there were 672,960 individual old age pensioners getting the maximum supplement, and 110,176 old age pension couples receiving the maximum supplement. In other words, just less than 45 per cent of all old age pensioners were getting the full supplement and the full benefit of the 2 per cent cost of living escalator.
If the Liberal government had lived up to its promise in 1968 of a "just society" and given the old age pensioners and those on guaranteed income supplement an amount equivalent to the annual rise in the cost of living, the old age pension would have gone from $75 per month to $89.85 today-this shows how the pensioner has been gypped-and the guaranteed income supplement would have gone from $30 to $58.81. In 1972, individual recipients of the old age security pension would be receiving $9.85 more a month or $118.20 more per year than they actually do now. That is this magnanimous government. Similarly, in 1972 all recipients of the guaranteed income supplement would be receiving $58.51 instead of the present level of $55, or putting it another way, this would mean over the year a difference of $42.12 to recipients of the maximum guaranteed income supplement. The total cost of this program from January 1, 1968, to December 31, 1971, would have amounted to $230 million. The money was there, Mr. Speaker, because on December 31, 1971, there was a balance of $636 million in the old age security fund.
Now, I intend to deal with those people for a few minutes and show how they get by, because it is apparent that some members of the government think these pensioners live in luxury. The average rent for a bachelor

apartment in any of our cities or towns today is $125 a month whilst a one bedroom apartment, runs at an average of $150 per month. I have checked those figures. I leave it to the reasoning and common sense of members of this House to decide how these people live. Just how do they get by? In a city of approximately 22,000 people, typical of old Ontario, there are 15 single units renting at $37 a month and 12 units for married couples. These are subsidized, but to qualify one must have an income of $175 a month or less. I also checked these figures. Hundreds of applications are on record for low-cost housing. In that city, Mr. Speaker, there were 2,349 old age pensioners and over 1,500 of them were getting the guaranteed income supplement. I do not think I need dwell further on the bind in which those people found themselves. When you consider that, on the average, they have to spend 28 per cent of income on food and 25 per cent on shelter, you wonder how they live and by how much they must tighten their belts.
I have brought this motion forward today because of the cynical attitude taken by the government towards all government pensioners. What rhyme or reason is there for denying people their rights? What sort of government is it that will compensate people with dollars constantly eroded by inflation?

speechtext:
This payment is not charity. It has been paid for in taxes and there is at present a surplus of over $600 million in the fund. As I said, the older people paid into the fund in hard dollars. Yet each year the dollar purchases less. The former minister of finance, who is now Minister of National Defence (Mr. Benson), estimated that there would be over $2 billion available for 1970-71. He only paid out $1,905 million; what did he do with the balance of $95 million?
We cheat those on fixed incomes when we pay them in cheapened dollars. I wonder how much has been taken out of the OHSIP fund in the form of taxes on doctor's incomes; to what extent have medical services been taxed? When we tax the inflated incomes of certain doctors, we are placing a tax on sickness. As I said, we cheat those on fixed incomes when we pay them in cheapened dollars. Do not forget, Mr. Speaker, that inflation yields more revenue for the government through higher salaries.
March 23, 1972

Nevertheless, the government has frozen the old age pension. They now call our pensioners the "Trudeau rich". I do not know who invented that label. There are about 510,000 of them in this country; I am speaking of pensioners with incomes of between $130 and $400 a month. During the past year their purchasing power declined by between $76 and $80.
If the government has been able to do this and get away with it, one wonders what else it can get away with. May I read from an editorial that appeared not long ago in the Globe and Mail. It reads:
Old-age pensions are not charity. They are not hand-outs by a compassionate Government to the destitute old. They are annuities returned to persons past 65 for investments, both direct and indirect, which the Government has compelled them to make year after year. The explanatory papers attached to Finance Minister Edgar Benson's budget speech made this clear. The country, which is at present making out its income tax returns, needs no reminder.
Each individual, as he works his way through his difficult tax return, will find that he is paying a 4 per cent tax on his taxable income, to a maximum of $240 per person per year, which is specifically earmarked for old-age security.
The article refers to a $600 million surplus in the fund, mentions the mothers allowance and blind persons allowance, and then reads:
But the basic old-age pensions were bought and paid for by the people who are collecting them.
They are collecting them, however, in money which year after year buys less and less.
The fact has not had the impact in this House that it ought to have had. Some wage earners who paid into the pension fund earned $35 a week in hard dollars. Now, some of our people are earning up to eight times as much; others, of course, are not earning quite that much. We said to the old age pensioner, if the cost of living goes up by more than 2 per cent, the old age security pension will be escalated by 2 per cent per year, maximum. Mr. Speaker, I believe Your Honour was a legal light. How would an agreement stand up in court if it provided for an increase of 2 per cent in pensions if the cost of living went up by more than 2 per cent, but not a nickel extra if it went up by less than 2 per cent? Would that not be considered as a one-sided agreement? Yet the cost of living has been rising at 4 and 5 per cent per year, and the buying power of our older people has been shrinking by about 3 per cent per year. Prices go up but pensions do not match that rise. Is that not unfair? Taking the hard earned dollars of working people who paid into the fund in hard cash and paying them with inflated dollars is also unfair. One could go on enumerating grievances.
As I said, if the government could do this in the case of pensioners, one wonders what it could do with bonds or securities of any kind. The government has broken its agreement. Mr. Speaker, perpetual bonds issued in 1935 are now worth only 40 cents on the dollar. This indicates how much their worth has shrunk. If that does not bring about distrust of government, I do not know what will. Is that the sort of honesty the government is preaching to the people of Canada? I say to the government that it creates deep distrust in the minds of Canadians by reneging on old agreements and by refusing to give the old age pensioner his rightful due. The government knows full well that rents and the cost of shelter went up last year by
Pension Increases
7 per cent and that food went up by 7 per cent. Knowing all this, why does the government deny our older people justice? The government takes the view that if the rate of inflation is 2 per cent per year or more, the pension of the pensioner will increase by 2 per cent. However, if the rate of inflation is under 2 per cent, the pensioner gets no increase. That is a pretty one-sided contract.
May I say a few words about family allowances? I expect hon. members recall that family allowances first came on the scene in 1945 when the average weekly wage in Canada was $32.50. Now, the average weekly wage has multiplied by four times to $132.72. That was the 1970 level, and represents an increase of approximately 400 per cent. Family allowances, on the other hand, have increased by only 15 per cent since 1945. How are family allowances to be dealt with? A family with one child between one and 11 years of age is to get $180, and $240 if the child is between 12 and 17. These amounts are not as great as they should be. They are at about 75 per cent of the level that would be fair.
The joke here is that they are shortchanging the family 25 per cent. There is no cost of living allowance written in, nor any escalator clause. That remains fixed. All you have to do is look around at the money that is being brought into circulation. The money supply in this country was increased by 30 percent in January and 40 percent in February. This means only one thing. We are going to have runaway inflation. It may take a few months to catch up, but it will catch up. There is no escalator clause. This party would like to see such a clause put in the family allowance scheme.
Knowing how cynically this government refused the old age pension adjustments, it is important that we do not let this government get away with anything. The same holds true for pensioners in other areas. They see the salaries of their counterparts being driven up by the fires of inflation away beyond what they ever received. They also see themselves limited to an escalator clause which is away below the inflationary figure of just under 5 percent.
I now want to deal briefly with veterans affairs. First, there is a lack of an escalator clause in pensions paid to veterans to compensate for the increase in the cost of living. This House dealt with the Hong Kong veteran. I had the privilege of examining some of those veterans. Their pension increase was long overdue because of the inhumane way they had been treated. However, do hon. members know that we have not done a solitary thing for the fellow who fought in other areas of war, those who fought in Europe, were manacled and chained in Europe, went on forced marches and starved. We have never done one solitary thing about their problems.

This means that old age pensioners drawing the guaranteed income supplement, and who now get a 2 per cent increase a year, would get a 5 or 6 per cent increase in line with the increase in the cost of living. I would hope, also, that the motion would be regarded as covering certain other pensioners, for example, those of the Canadian National-they do not come directly under the government but they work for a Crown corporation. Once we get into that area we also think of Canadian Pacific employees and others. I trust I am not doing an injustice to the motion when I say that what it asks for is that all pension arrangements should contain an escalator clause and that the escalation should not be limited to 2 per cent but that it be equivalent to the actual rise in the cost of living.

Mr. Speaker, I always welcome a debate on pensions. I always welcome any plea made by any hon. member in any quarter of the House for an improvement in the lot of our senior citizens and retired people. But I have to say I am bitterly disappointed, today, because the Progressive Conservative party has not gone far enough. This motion today is in line with the kind of thing the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) has been saying as he has gone about the country during the last few weeks, namely that the federal

March 23, 1972
Pension Increases
government is not doing enough for old age pensioners. But when he gets down to something precise, he says exactly the same as that put forward in this motion, namely that the pensions of our retired citizens should be increased, not just by 2 per cent but by the full amount of the increase in the cost of living. That means an increase of 5 or 6 per cent. It means that those now drawing $80 a month will get another $4 or $5. It means that those now drawing $135 a month will get another $6.75. It means for those on war veterans allowance, who are receiving, if single, $121 a month, an increase in the order of $6.
I say that is not good enough, Mr. Speaker. It is a delusion to create the impression that simply by adding to pensions in step with the increase in the cost of living you have done your duty by the senior citizens and pensioners of this country. What is sorely needed and is long overdue is an upward adjustment in the basic rates of all these pensions. Shame on the Liberals for doing nothing, but shame on the Progressive Conservatives for asking only for a 5 or 6 per cent increase in the present $80 pension! The pension should be raised to $150 a month. Veterans should not be on an allowance, if single, of $121 a month, or $201 a month, if married; those allowances should be at least $150 a month single and $300 a month for a married veteran.
I could go on down the list. Pensions of all kinds presently being paid under the auspices of the government need to be reviewed, and the question asked: Are they of a reasonable amount in light of today's production, today's cost of living and today's standard of living? When you talk merely of increasing pensions in relation to the cost of living, Mr. Speaker, all you are doing is permitting older people to continue to enjoy whatever standard of living we gave them when we fixed their pension. The fact is that when we fixed their pensions we put them into the poverty bracket, and all you do by raising pensions in step with the increase of the cost of living is to keep those pensioners within the same poverty bracket. That in itself is bad enough. But, in addition to that, by increasing pensions simply by that amount we are saying to our retired citizens: "This is a wonderful age. Production is going up, standards of living are going up, people are living more affluent lives, but you older folks are not to share in those things; you have to stay with the 'keep body and soul together' pattern rather than share in the increase in our country's standard of living".
What we should be asking for today is for the raising of the basic amounts of all pensions. Before I get to the end of my time-and I am keeping my eye on the clock, Mr. Speaker-I shall be moving an amendment to this effect. I do not intend to move it at this moment but I might read it so that hon. members will know what is coming. When I reach the end of my twenty minutes, I shall move that the motion be amended by adding thereto, immediately after the word "Canada", the following words:
-and its failure to raise to adequate levels the basic amounts of all such pensions, allowances and benefits.
If my amendment were accepted, the motion as amended would then read:

That this House condemns the government's failure to contribute to pensions, allowances and other benefits granted or administered by the government a yearly percentage increase corresponding to the percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index for Canada, and its failure to raise to adequate levels the basic amounts of all such pensions, allowances and benefits.
I should have liked to recast the motion and to put the question of raising the basic amounts first, then calling for the full scale escalation clause, but I was afraid I would get into procedural trouble if I did that. However, the result is the same if I put my amendment at the end of the main motion. What I want this House to face up to this afternoon is not only the shame of the government for failing to do anything for the pensioners of this country, but to the inadequacy of the proposal that has come from the official opposition which asks merely for an increase equal to the increase in the cost of living.
Our position is that our old age pensioners today should have as a very minimum a pension of $150 a month; that that $150 a month should then be escalated year by year as the cost of living goes up. Starting from that level, an increase of 5 or 6 per cent would mean something. But 5 or 6 per cent of the present $80 a month, or even of the $135 that the guaranteed income supplement pensioners receive, is hopelessly inadequate. We also contend that veterans allowances and war disability pensions should be reviewed. I was pleased with the answer I got from the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Laing) the other day to the effect that consideration is being given to the representations that have been made by War Amputations of Canada for an increase in the basic rate of war disability pensions, and I hope the minister meant what he said.
The fact of the matter is that the basic rate of the war disability pension, which was set just after World War I at a certain wage standard in the Public Service, has fallen behind that standard. I also draw attention to the fact that the war veterans allowance today for a single person is only $121 a month, or $201 a month for a married veteran. Certainly, that is not good enough, even if other income up to $161 single and $271 married is permitted. Neither is it good enough just to ask for those amounts to be increased by the extent to which the cost of living has risen. I insist that those figures should be at least $150 for a single veteran and $300 for one who is married. As hon. members know, I believe we should do even better and provide a guaranteed income at an adequate level to all veterans at age 55.
I have already referred to the pensions of retired public servants. I am still excited over the fact that we finally won for them the principle of an increase in their pension after those affected have retired. I think the initial step taken by the government in 1970, providing for a considerable amount of retroactivity, was a good one; I said so then and I say so again today. But in the meantime we have had a substantial rise in the cost of living which has outdistanced the 2 per cent increases that these people have received. Salaries have gone up, to the extent that today future pensions are going to be larger than the amount many former public servants drew as salary. This is why it is time the basic amounts of pensions that people are receiving today should be reviewed. It is also time, as I have said, for the escalation rate to be raised from 2 per cent to the actual rate of increase taking place.
March 23, 1972

In the case of the Canada Pension Plan I think there, too, the 2 per cent ceiling has to be reviewed and revised. I concede that some time ago the government did put on the records of this House the appropriate notices so that this matter could be discussed by the federal and provincial governments. I hope that those discussions will be actively carried forward, because a great deal has happened to our economy since the Canada Pension Plan was introduced-and I was one of those who supported it, there is no question of that-which requires the plan's benefits to be jacked up. Here again it is not going to be enough just to ask for the amount of escalation that is proposed in the motion before the House today; we must review the basic rates.
I could go on and mention again the Canadian National pensions and Canadian Pacific pensions, as well as industrial pensions generally. I repeat the plea that I have made many a time on the floor of this House that we amend the Pension Benefits Standards Act to require industrial pensions to meet the standards we are talking about today.
The point I am trying to make at this time is that though welcoming, as I do, the motion set down this afternoon by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard), I feel the real problem that not only this parliament but society has to face is this: It is no longer good enough to treat our older people as objects of charity. It is no longer good enough simply to say to them: "We have given you a certain level of pension and we shall maintain you at that level by increasing your pension to the extent the cost of living increases". The time has come when basic rates have to be adjusted, and they will have to be readjusted every four or five years.
The plain fact is that if we have a humane and decent civilization our older people have just as much right to share in the rising standard of living as those involved in producing it. A further point I have made on other occasions, and will make it again as I get the opportunity, is that we must now be thinking about lowering the pensionable age. At least we should be providing that full old age security and Canada Pension Plan benefits should be available to our people at age 60 on one condition only, namely, that they leave the labour market. This would mean a great deal to these people. Many people at that age with the other savings or pensions they have would retire if given that opportunity, and this would do something to create jobs for the younger people. There is no question but that our attempt to raise the living standards of our people in the older age brackets would call for the production of more goods and services. Those who oppose us would like to knock down our idea by saying this would cost too much. What it will cost is more production and this would mean putting more people to work in order to produce the goods. A good and decent pension program would not only do something for our older people but would also have an advantageous effect on our economy as a whole and make things better for all people including our younger people who are sorely in need of jobs today.
I see my time is running out. There are one or two points I should like to make before I move the amendment I have already read. There is only one set of statistics to which I want to refer. It is the same set of statistics the
Pension Increases
hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard) used in the opening part of his speech. His figures contained one error. This, however, was not his fault. He quoted a figure from page 949 of Hansard for March 20 which was part of a set of answers to questions of mine. The figure he quoted happens to be wrong. I drew attention to it as a matter of privilege on March 21 and I have been assured by the department that it will be corrected some time soon. I should like therefore, to refer to the figures put on Hansard of March 20 with the correction to which I have referred. The figures show that 1,756,548 Canadians are drawing old age security. That presumably just about equals the number of Canadians who are over 65, counting all but those who do not have sufficient residence to qualify for the pension.
Of that number 978,068 qualify for some portion of the guaranteed income supplement. That figure is 55 per cent of the total. In other words, more than half of the people of Canada who are over 65 years of age are so poor and so needy that they now receive some portion of the guaranteed income supplement. I shall go on further. The hon. member for Simcoe North gave a figure of 110,805. That is the wrong figure which will be corrected in a few days. It should be 484,394. That is the number of people receiving the full amount. I think it is a disgrace and we should bow our heads in shame, for that figure represents 27 per cent of the people of Canada who are over age 65. Remember that in order to qualify for the full amount of the guaranteed income supplement one can have nothing else. One might have $2 or something like that, but for all practical purposes he can have nothing else. That means that of the people who today in this tremendous and wonderful land reach age 65, more than one in every four reach it in a state of destitution. They have nothing. They are able to qualify not only for old age security which presently is $80 a month, but are able to qualify for the full amount of the guaranteed income supplement.
If anything ever demonstrated the need for a massive increase in what we are doing for pensioners these figures do it. I see my time is running out and therefore perhaps I should move my amendment before I am called upon to sit down. I want to say again that I welcome this motion even though I have been critical and have expressed some disappointment at my friends in the Progressive Conservative party for asking for so little. We shall vote for the motion because it is the least that should be done, but I hope other members of the House will join with us tonight in voting for our amendment. It says not only do we want escalation according to the cost of living but we want the basic amounts of all pensions across the board to be reviewed and raised to adequate levels. As an example of what we mean by the motion, we are asking that the basic amount of the old age pension be raised right now to not less than $150 a month.
Therefore, I have pleasure in moving, seconded by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas):
That the motion be amended by adding thereto, immediately after the word "Canada", the following words:

March 23, 1972
Pension Increases
"and its failure to raise to adequate levels the basic amounts of
all such pensions, allowances and benefits".

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INCREASE   PENSIONS BY SAME PERCENTAGE AS INCREASE IN CONSUMER PRICE INDEX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is my duty to take part in the debate on the motion now before the House which reads:
That this House condemns the government's failure to contribute to pensions, allowances and other benefits granted or administered by the government a yearly percentage increase corresponding to the percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index for Canada.
I would begin my comments by mentioning two typical examples which will enable us to understand the problem.
A senior citizen of 65 came to my office in Victoriaville recently. He is severely ill and is receiving an old pension of $135 a month. He pays $70 for rent per month, which is reasonable, but he is left with only $65 a month for food, clothing and drugs.
This senior citizen is trying by every means to obtain supplementary assistance from provincial departments but to no avail, since he is told by officials that his case is the responsibility, not of the provincial government, but of the federal government from which he receives an old age pension. Anyway, every endeavour this citizen has made has been doomed to failure. In addition, he is unable to buy the necessary drugs to cure his sickness.
This a health matter of health but he is unable to buy them. The prevailing system prevents him from obtaining these drugs.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if we do not urgently take effective steps to solve this problem we are all somewhat responsible for this citizen's predicament and even for his death, because if we refuse, as a society, to increase this aid we will all have contributed to someone's misfortune and perhaps to his death.
This case is not unique. My hon. friends are well aware that hundreds of cases like this exist in Canada but that the resources to satisfy the needs of these people are non-existent.
Let us consider another case, Mr. Speaker, that of two people who each receive a maximum pension, including the guaranteed income supplement. It gives them a total income of $255. In order to get that maximum amount, their marginal income must be minimum. In other words, after paying a reasonable rent of $70 a month, they are left with $185 a month or $46 a week, which makes $23 per person, to buy food, clothes, drugs and essential items.
If their television set-their only enjoyment-breaks down, they do not have enough to have it repaired. The same goes for essential appliances such as their refrigerator, their stove, etc.
What will we do for them, Mr. Speaker? Will we stop talking about them once and for all and take action? I am very pleased to have this debate today since it will allow us all to ask ourselves that question.
The main objective of the motion before us today is to have pensions paid to those in need, to the needy, escalat-

ed in the same proportion as the increase in the cost of living.
Mr. Speaker, I have here a clipping from the newspaper La Presse of Tuesday, March 21, 1972, entitled "Trend in recent months points to renewed inflation".
Two conclusions may be drawn. First, the fight against inflation by the government in the past four years has been conducted at the expense of the low income people and has certainly not solved the problem. Just the opposite. Second, this fight has contributed directly to the increase in the seasonally-adjusted rate of unemployment and neither unemployment nor inflation have been stopped.
The conclusion was drawn that the fight against inflation has been a monumental failure and finally, the conclusion can also be drawn that those benefiting from federal social welfare programs-which will cost this year, if I am right, $619 million according to the booklet "How your tax dollar is spent" published under the authority of the Treasury Board-will not be in a position tomorrow to meet another increase in the cost of living.
According to this newspaper report, the index of beef prices has gone up. Well, that is a product necessary for elderly and poor people. We are told that the index of general consumer prices has increased, and also that the price of eggs has increased, although most egg producers are going bankrupt because of the new program. It also says that pork prices are up.
All these developments apply to both the rich and the poor in our society. For the well-to-do, there is no great difficulty in adjusting to increased cost of living and inflation, but those who have no resources, no source of extra income because they are disabled or old, are the first victims of the increase in the cost of living. And what is being done for these people? Are we merely going to talk about it? Will we do something about it, some day.
What is most expensive now? Clothes, food, shelter and finally drugs. Well, those four items I have just mentioned are those which have most consistently increased in price during the past four years. This responsible article in La Presse states that the rise in prices will continue and accelerate until it gets out of control, which, as a matter of fact, is what is now happening.
Mr. Speaker, it is high time to see to this problem. The old, the poor, the disabled need shelter, food, clothes and drugs and you will agree with me, Mr. Speaker, that the assistance meted out to them, $135 for old age pension, with a maximum of $255 for two, is ludicrous.
Unemployment, increasingly frequent closing down of factories are all problems resulting from economic deficiencies. Today's unemployment in Canada, resulting from anti-inflation measures and creating cost of living problems, is not a consequence of saturated consumer demand or of exhaustion of production resources, but solely of nondistribution of products and services. There is no scarcity of products in Canada, Mr. Speaker. In the west, there is a wheat surplus problem. In Quebec, there are milk, butter and egg surpluses, surpluses of everything. The problem in Quebec is one of overproduction, according to learned government experts. In the Maritimes, there again they have surpluses of everything. How is it
March 23, 1972

that at the very time when there are surpluses of everything in Canada, poverty is increasing while unemployment and the cost of living continue to rise?
Mr. Speaker, to realize fully the need for an increase in old age security pensions to a reasonable level, in keeping with the cost of living, several factors should be taken into consideration. There is something I should like to mention, on the occasion of this speech, to stress the necessity of increasing old age pensions.
Canada draws its wealth from four main sources: the soil, subsoil, forests and waters. Our subsoil is so rich, Mr. Speaker, that it would be quicker to list the minerals that we do not find in it than those we do find. Therefore, the problem is not there.
Our soil is so rich that, as I said earlier, there are surpluses everywhere, in the west, in the east, in the Maritimes and in the central provinces. There is also a surplus of wheat, milk, fish, etc.
Our forests are so rich that they could be classed into two main categories: hardwoods and softwoods. The problem may be there. We have so much softwood, Mr. Speaker, that we do not know what to do with it. The main industries in that field are shutting down and laying off workers. So, the problem is not there since we have too much softwood. What about hardwood? Our stock is so plentiful that over the past 99 years we did not even have the courage to ensure the regrowth of our forests. We had so much of it that we gave it to the Americans, to foreigners, under extended 99-year leases. Again the problem does not lie there either. But where is it since we have so many resources? In our oceans, in our fisheries? Well, if we listen to the minister and study government statistics, we find out that here again we have surpluses.
In Denmark, a wee little country with a very high standard of living, at least favourably comparable with ours, they can count on one single resource: their subsoil. We on the other hand have at least four important groups of resources.
Japan has become the third commercial power in the world with a population of 122 million inhabitants living in 12 small cities. We Canadians have 22 million people thinly spread over one of the largest country in the world and so many resources that we do not know how to cope with them, yet we tolerate some one million unemployed.
We tolerate the fact that three families out of five are poor, according to the conclusions of the Croll report on poverty.
We have just begun implementing a tax reform establishing the poverty level at $3,000. On the other hand, we are not providing $3,000 a year for our old people to enable them to live decently. If we believe that the poverty level is at $3,000, let us give at least that strict minimum to the older people. I am almost ashamed to ask such a thing. That would not solve their problem, but their pension would almost be double what it is now.
Mr. Speaker, we must stop wasting our riches, stop deceiving citizens with hopes of creating employment. According to the brochure "How your tax dollar is spent", millions and millions are spent to create employment.
Pension Increases
Creating employment has become a mania. And as the government says: Let us create jobs or offers grants to create jobs, it adds in the same breath: We have too much wheat; let us set quotas. We have too many products in the east, let us establish ceilings. As a matter of fact, we have too much of everything. That is why there are so many things on the shelves of the department stores. While investing millions of dollars to create employment, the government says: Starve, for there are too many products.
Mr. Speaker, that shows that the problem lies nowhere but in a fair allocation of riches in Canada. Some may find that funny, but older and disabled people do not.
And, as I said in an earlier speech, the Unemployment Insurance Act itself-and do consider the sincerity of my remarks-is fine. Weekly benefits range up to $100, which shows that the government recognizes the impossibility of living with less in Canada. This legislation is fine in itself, but when we put it in the social and economic context in which we are compelled to live, we must conclude that it is more profitable to work nine months a year and to draw social welfare benefits or to be unemployed for the rest of the year than to work 12 months a year. We have reached the point where unemployment directly competes with work. And, meanwhile, poverty and wealth keep on increasing in Canada and there is no contact between the rich and the poor.
Mr. Speaker, our surplus production should be fairly distributed among all Canadians. Social Credit advocates a program whose purpose is to fill at all times the gap between prices of products offered to the consumers and the money in the hands of the consumers who want to get those products which they made. Such a system therefore rules out both inflation and deflation. It automatically and mathematically maintains balance between production and purchasing power. It puts money at the service of the people and forces them to assume their role, that is disposing of the production to the satisfaction of the consumer inasmuch as natural and industrial resources allow.
The Social Credit party is very funny but I can assure the House that the system that has been defended for 100 years is no longer funny. The Social Credit party is also a dedicated protector of ownership, of private enterprise. Any private enterprise has a social function to fulfill, which will inevitably be accomplished through a financial system consistent with the Creditiste proposals which advocate justice in distribution.
So, I say to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that he will never come through with a just society in Canada unless he examines the proposals regarding justice in distribution. People are fooling themselves if they do not consider distribution of wealth. What is justice? It is fair distribution or equal consideration for all Canadians. This is exactly what we are asking for.
Any individual has the triple right to life, liberty, pursuit of happiness in a free country with decent standards. This is why, Mr. Speaker, we are asking for this system. The guarantee of such a right rests on the undeniable possibility of producing today all the things necessary to their achievement by using only a fraction of the human potential.

March 23, 1972
Pension Increases
However, in the system that has been protected for 100 years-and you will see how this can be ridiculous-yesterday's production is bought today with tomorrow's money.
This is why most Canadians are in debt up to their neck for over $17 billion. We say, as far as today's production goes, let us buy it today and pay it today to bring this never-ending indebtedness to an end.
Mr. Speaker, we are deceiving ourselves if we believe that getting deeper into debt is the way out of our indebtedness. Anyone interested can obtain the pamphlet offered by the federal government and read at page 24 that Canada's public debt stands at $46 billion-not counting private indebtedness-and that this debt eats up 14 cents of each tax dollar paid by Canadians. This year alone, it will cost us $2,160 million in interests.
That is the financial system we are protecting. For whom? For our senior citizens? No, Mr. Speaker. For the disabled? No, Mr. Speaker. For the have nots? No, Mr. Speaker. When those people reach old age they do not face the problems which plague our senior citizens.
I would like to conclude with this: to understand the potentialities of the monetary system proposed by the Social Credit Party, let us not forget that the world is now in an era of affluence and thats-if we have poverty it is not because there are rich people but because this affluence is not equally distributed. Therefore, no need at all to strip the rich from their wealth and give it to the poor; let us simply put some technique into the monetary system and stop repeating that money is made for man. What we should do is put money to the service of man.
Mr. Speaker, we have two choices: Either we keep on degrading people or we take the steps required to encourage individuals to build and develop their country. Either we keep on protecting high finance with our citizens as slaves or we keep high finance down and we put money to the service of the Canadian people.
I will conclude by asking two questions. Why are we so afraid in this House of a monetary reform? Why are we prepared to reform anything except our monetary system?
I would like someone to reply, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a good deal of interest to the spokesmen for the opposition parties on the other side of the House, in particular to the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard) who, I think, very properly has brought a well-founded resolution before the House concerning the problem of pension adjustments in a period of inflation. This is a problem which all western societies have to face now.
Indeed the record of Canada in regard to price controls in this period of, shall we say, price stability, according to recent studies has been as good as that of any of the 14 western European nations examined. But our record is not good enough. The government, with its responsibilities, has the very difficult problem of trying to create a

delicate balance between price stability and employment. So far as pensions are concerned, the problem is particularly acute. It is difficult to maintain the degree of price stability that we would all like to see because, in view of the record of our major trading partners, we generally have to stay in step with them or else pressures show up in our balance of payments, in our foreign exchange rates, and so on. But in spite of the great difficulty in maintaining a temperate degree of price stability, the problem of adjustment of pensions has to be faced. It can be faced in two ways: either in terms of an automatic escalation formula, for which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has fought as have other members of this House or it can be faced by discretionary adjustments over a period of time. This has been the procedure in the case of the Department of Veterans Affairs.
Before discussing in more detail the adjustments for pensions, war veterans allowance and war pensions, I should like to make a few general remarks about the kind of statement we have heard today. My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre, who is in the House at present, accused the opposition party that moved the motion of not promising enough and he did a magnificent job of out-promising them. He said that pensions should not merely be escalated for the cost of living but that the old age pension should be brought up to the basic level of $150 a month and the age limit lowered to 60 years. I think this is a fair summary of one of his recommendations. Mr. Speaker, we have gone through this debate at other times in this House. If it were only as simple as that. If the only thing to be done was for members of this House to be kind and generous and pass the motion, then pensions would flow on unhindered. If life were that simple it would be very nice.
The fact is that sums of this magnitude are very consequential. I have made some calculation and it would take something in the order of $1} billion to increase the pension of everyone over the age of 65 to $150 a month. This is regardless of whether or not they get the supplement. I may be out in my calculations but I think that is approximately correct. Reducing the age from 65 to 60 would substantially increase the cost. I know that my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre says that costs do not matter but he knows that increased expenditures of that amount are inflationary unless drastic measures are taken to compensate with revenue from other sources. It is not enough to give everybody what they would like. Then, why stop at $150? If we were to approve it, the hon. member would raise his sights. The fact is that these proposals in themselves are inflationary. It is like trying to solve the problem of putting out the fire by throwing gasoline on it. To those pensioners suffering from the increase in the cost of living, it is no compensation to promise measures which cannot be enacted consistent with even that degree of price stability which we have today.
As I indicated, Mr. Speaker, the Department of Veterans Affairs has been concerned about the problem and over a period of time has undertaken to adjust those pension rates which fall within its jurisdiction. Hon. members will recall that on March 17, in reply to a question from the hon. member from Winnipeg North Centre, the
March 23, 1972

Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Laing) stated that consideration is being given to representations by the War Amputations of Canada asking for an increase in basic rates of pensions. He further stated that, while basic rates of war veterans allowance are not presently under review, "an action taken in one place might have consequences in another". The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is smiling, but this is precisely the exchange that took place.

I should add that the minister met with representatives of the association a few weeks ago. For some years it has been the practice of the government to review basic rates of both pensions and war veterans allowances once in about every two years, and to make any adjustments that might appear warranted.
Pursuant to this policy, basic rates of pension were raised by 11.1 per cent, effective September 1, 1964. Two years later, on September 1, 1966, the rates were again increased by 15 per cent. Just 16 months later, on January 1, 1968, the pension rates were raised by 15.2 per cent. Finally, just a year ago, on April 1, 1971, the basic rates of pension were again raised by 10 per cent. At the present time a 100 per cent pensioner, married and with one child, receives a pension of $4,920 a year. In addition, he may receive an exceptional incapacity allowance of up to $2,400 per annum under the provisions of last year's amendments to the Pension Act-I want to come back to this in a moment-and a further amount of up to $3,000 a year in attendance allowance. All these amounts are exempt from income tax. Furthermore, I have already indicated that the matter of basic rates of pension is under review again.
Summarizing the situation on disability pensions, I would point out that, considering only the basic rates and ignoring all the other supplementary payments, pension rates during the ten years between 1961 and 1971 have risen by 67 per cent, while consumer prices rose by only half as much, 33 per cent.
The position with respect to basic rates of war veterans allowance is very similar. On September 1, 1964 they were increased by 11.9 per cent. Exactly two years later on September 1, 1966, they went up by 11.7 per cent. A year ago, on April 1, 1971, these basic rates were raised by 15 per cent. Taking together the increases of the ten-year period from April 1, 1961 to April 1, 1971, the rise in basic rates of war veterans allowance has also been more than double the rise in consumer prices.
In the financial estimates for the year 1972-73, a sum of $232,550,000 has been requested for the payment of disability pensions and pensions to survivors, and a further $781 million for the payment of war veterans allowance. In addition, a sum of $8 \ million is being provided under the assistance fund regulations, to give supplementary financial help to those individual cases whose needs may not be fully met through the war veterans allowance program. Some people will say there is no sum of money that will fully compensate those who have risked their health or their lives in the defence of their country, and I would not deny this argument for a moment. The fact remains, however, that both disability pensioners and recipients of
Pension Increases
war veterans allowance are very much better off financially as a result of the adjustments over a period of time.
I can only say this, Mr. Speaker, that as to the future, the government intends to keep faith with these veterans. Under the policy already established, a review of rates under both plans would be made and if changes appeared to be required, legislation would be introduced in order to authorize any adjustments.
I want to say a word or two about the exceptional incapacity allowance.
