The programs are not very satisfactory, but they are all that we have today. There is something significant about the concern of the hon. member. I am sure all hon. members here have had experiences similar to mine in dealing with the great problems that face us and that face, in particular, the two groups to whom we have referred. We know of the lack of jobs for many. This lack affects especially the young, and those who are well educated and well trained.
I am sure every one of us here has a dossier on young people trying to find employment. Day in and day out I am sure every one of us hears of the anxiety of our older citizens. At a time when tranquility, security and confidence should be theirs, they are fraught with anxiety, poverty and fear. Surely, these are appalling and shameful conditions. Someone said that the war on poverty may never have got under way and that the war on inflation was a failure. That war, however, found two victims, the unemployed man and the pensioner. In a great country as rich as Canada-and we can produce all sorts of statistics to show our national riches and national greatness-far, far too many people are living in poverty. We did not need

the Senate Committee to demonstrate to us that which we already know. Many thousands of Canadians face insecurity and inadequacy in this great land. Living costs are accelerating all the time. Rents are going up; all costs are rising and the value of the dollar is shrinking, ever shrinking. For most of the people we have in mind today, there are no great unions, no powerful pressure lobbies, no pressure groups; those people are the victims, the silent, sad victims of a grossly mismanaged economy.
If we heed all the portents and read the report of the Governor of the Bank of Canada, we will see that this group is in for even more hardship, because that report shows that our failure in the war on inflation will soon bring its baleful results. As the parliamentary secretary suggested, those people about whom we are concerned have too often become footballs and their plight has too often been an area of neglect. It was one of the great indications of public disfavour when a former Liberal government fell after it had revealed a unique and cold lack of compassion. At that time the six buck slogan helped to bring to an end a government which had lost compassion and concern for the poor of this country.

Mr. Speaker, there are hundreds of thousands of unfortunate Canadians today, and if you tell them they never had it so good, you will get a reaction that is far from positive, let me assure you.
This resolution covers many people; the old, those who require security most. Instead of that, they are expressing frustration and insecurity. It concerns the veterans. They are getting older and their job opportunities are diminishing. The costs of their daily needs are increasing. I say to the parliamentary secretary that he can put forward statistics all day and all night, but I know that thousands and thousands of these people are not getting enough. They must and should get more. Let us not monkey around with statistics.
If I had time, and I do not have time today, I could point out that there are countries in the world which do a far better job for their veterans than this country. One simple indicator is that the basic rate for veterans pensions in the United States is $5,400, almost $2,000 more than Canada's basic rate of $3,504. Let the government spokesman stick out his chest over that. Time and again we run across the problems of the widow with a young dependant who is not yet through university. The other day I received a call about a fine young man with just one more year to go to obtain his University degree, but his student allowance is to be cut off. Where does the widow turn? Some hon. members who spoke before me mentioned former civil servants and other groups who are bottled in and suppressed in an economic pressure tank. Something must be done for them.
One problem that has troubled many of us, again in connection with veterans, is the heavy backlog which faces the Canada Pension Commission. I think this is a fine group of civil servants, but they cannot cope with 1,000 applications a month and do justice to them. For months the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) has been appealing for additional help for the Canada Pension Commission to get through the backlog. As these veterans wait, they are not getting any richer or any younger. They are not getting action. Some of them are dying. This is the kind of thing a government of compassion would do.
There is no shortage of personnel when the government wants to expand the office of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). Surely, a few can be found to assist the Canada Pension Commission. This is a very serious question in
Pension Increases
every part of the country, including my own. The parliamentary secretary may represent an area where everybody is content with what they get and happy when told that they are getting more than ever before. However, I have received statistics from what should be called the Dominion Bureau of Statistics but what is now called Statistics Canada. These indicate that in the city of Charlottetown, a place for which for many years it was difficult to get precise statistics, the cost of living has increased from January 1969 by 11.3 points in comparison with 6.4 for Saint John and 3.8 for Halifax.
When we ask why Prince Edward Island is excluded from the increase in feed grain subsidies, no one even bothers to give us a reply. When we talk about the transportation problems which increase the cost of living, we discover that there were 29 increases in freight rates in eight years. There is a lack of sensitivity, a lack of compassion and a lack of concern. Surely, it is the government's role in a society like ours to be the friend of those who need friends, those who suffer from the economic system most.
We talk about regional disparities, but surely disparity between groups of citizens must also be looked after as a number one priority of the government. I call upon those who momentarily occupy the seats of office in this country to take note of the wise, thoughtful suggestions contained in this motion and the compassion restraint and moderate tones with which the very eloquent, dedicated member who moved it suggested they be accomplished. The government should transcend politics for once and allow the old, the dispossessed, the poor and the struggling to see the House of Commons at its best.

We realize that its intent is to help the old people of this country and those retired people on pension. To this extent, we favour it. However, we want to point out that between the intent and the effect there is a big difference. To merely put an escalator clause in effect at this time would do very little to rescue the elderly people from the strait jacket in which they find themselves. Nothing can rescue them from that except a revision of the basic pension.
My colleague, who more than any other man has the right to be called "the pensions advocate of the House of Commons", has already outlined the three elements which are essential in determining a basic pension. First, it should be set in relation to the cost of living. Second, it should be set in relation to the productivity of the country and, third, in relation to the standard of living prevriling in the country at the time. The escalator clause is the final feature which is necessary on top of such a basic pension. It makes sense.
I wish to refer to a letter which I recently received from an old age pensioner in Vancouver. I quote:

March 23, 1972
Pension Increases
We got notice recently of a projected raise of 2 per cent but which will not take effect for us till May 1st, 1972. The raise mentioned was not only ridiculously low but why mention it so far ahead when they are nearly 30 per cent behind in the cost of living index now.
I suggest to the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) that the elderly people in this country are not being taken in by his dextrous use of figures with regard to the cost of living and the escalator clause. The hon. member said there were a number of occasions when there had been a raise in the basic pension. Yes, the old age pension in particular has been raised on those occasions when it became politically dangerous not to do so, but never has the old age pension been set in relation to those factors I have mentioned. I challenge members on the government side to tell us what studies were made into any of those factors in setting the basic old age pension at any time in its history.
The hon. member for Ottawa West also referred to the fact of the government adopting the policy of discretionary adjustments. I think he may have been referring to veterans' pensions at that time. The party to which I belong is not at all enamoured of the way discretionary adjustments work in the hands of the government. We want a fair basic pension as a matter of right, one which cannot be tampered with or denied. That is the only kind of pension that is any good to the retired people of this country.
Our position on this matter is that at the present time pensions should be fixed at $150 a month or $1,800 a year for a single person. That is still well below the poverty line worked out in 1969 according to the Bureau of Statistics. At that time the poverty line for a single person was set at $1,894 and for two persons at $3,157. If that was true in 1969, then, judging by the way in which the cost of living has risen since that time, the figure of $150 is too low. Our only reason for proposing it is that we felt we had better ask for a figure at least in the same stratosphere as that which the government might accept.
Spokesmen for the government tell us the country cannot afford an increase at this time. The best and quickest answer to that assertion was given by the hon. member for Simcoe-North (Mr. Rynard) when he told the House that at the end of 1971 there were $639 million in the old age security fund. He added that this money had been contributed by the elderly people of this country and that to leave it where it was, undistributed, while making excuses for not paying decent basic pensions at a reasonable amount, was cheating them. Yes, it is cheating them and deceiving them as well. As long as we have this sum of $639 million in the fund, we have no possible justification for saying we cannot afford an increase.
The old people are not stupid. They do not believe the nation cannot afford an increase. Expenditures in connection with the Bonaventure, the Avro Arrow and other things were mentioned this afternoon. I want to say, as did the hon. member for Simcoe North, that no difficulty was encountered when it came to raising the pensions substantially of members of the House of Commons and of the Senate. I voted against that particular measure and I have the distinction of belonging to the only party in this

House which voted against it. I think this is well worth recalling when we are considering whether or not we can afford the kind of action I am urging.
In the next two or three minutes I want to let the old people speak for themselves and give their own views about living on an old age pension at this time. I have no doubt that members in all parts of the House can produce similar letters. Here is one from St. Leonard in the Province of Quebec:
Dear Mrs. Maclnnis:
I wrote you last June about my pension troubles down here in our Belle Province. At that time I told you that my wife and I were getting $135 per month between us in my old age pension and supplements plus $14 per month from Quebec, between us, for medicines. My wife is only 64, so she gets no pension. She needs new glasses and her spinal brace fixed. I attend the hospital every month for blood tests and a check-up as I suffer from heart trouble and hardening of the arteries in my legs. We were getting $149 per month. In August, 1971 my $14 from Quebec was stopped. They said we were getting too much. I was getting my medicines at the hospital at cost price but on January 1, 1972 they stopped it on the grounds that the government was not helping them enough to meet the cost. Medicine now costs me an average of $14 per month. I wrote to Mr. Munro in Ottawa. He referred me to Quebec, so I wrote to Mr. Castonguay. He referred my letter to the local office in Montreal and they sent me and my doctor more forms to fill up. But that is months ago and I guess they are still studying them yet. I have been to see them as I had my bottom teeth out in February, 1971 and I need new glasses, which they say they will help me pay for. But I am still waiting, both for teeth and glasses.
Enclosed is a letter I received from the welfare office. I wish you could read it out to Mr. Trudeau and ask him whether this is his idea of a just society.
I shall be very glad to read it to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). He may find it in Hansard. This was the response from the authorities in the Province of Quebec:
Your needs were established as follows: food, clothing, personal necessities, $76; cost of room, $50; for a total sum of $126 per month. As your income from the old age pension is $135 monthly, you have an exceedent of $9 per month for your ordinary needs. However, if you need medication exceeding $9 a month for you and your wife, or a set of artificial teeth, take an appointment with your social security agent at your local office as soon as possible.
Instead of getting annoyed and saying that the Quebec authorities are failing to provide adequate supplementary benefits, and that sort of thing, I shall say that we, in this federal parliament, are squarely responsible for not having provided an old age pension which would have covered this man's needs adequately, and for not having reduced the pensionable age to 60 so that his poor wife could have adequate treatment for her dental and medical needs. The way we treat the old people is disgusting. Like the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Rowland), I am getting fed up with a government which sits smugly opposite and talks about how much better it is here than in Timbuctoo or other far off regions of the earth and does nothing to take the money which has accumulated in its coffers on trust for these people and use it to give them a decent pension.

We live on a basic pension of $80. We had an increase of $42 a few years ago.

The powers that be would be well-advised to hire a few old pensioners to steer things straight as there are a lot of brains among them lying dormant. The causes for being in these circumstances now is the result of past government actions as outlined above and government today is still on the same track of procrastinating to the detriment of the many by so few.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot tolerate that the situation of the Canadian people be made as appalling as some opposition members would like us to believe.
Pension Increases
The weakness of the non-confidence motion introduced today lies in a series of most important omissions. Mr. Speaker, it is unfair to have the Canadian people believe that this government does not deal with poverty in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, it is unfair to have the Canadian people believe that this government does not look after older people. It is unfair also to have the Canadian people believe that this government does not care for the underprivileged.
This government has published a white paper on income security for Canadians. The opposition members should be aware of that paper. It should be their Bible, so to speak, their bedside book, and having heard what some opposition members had to say this afternoon, I feel they must get acquainted with it. I intend to send it to them because I think that either they pretend to know it or, simply, they do not.
It must be stressed that the income security programs in Canada can be applied and remain useful only under a flourishing economy and price stability. Unless the system affords most employable individuals an opportunity to exercise their basic skills profitably, the national resources required for funding income security will fall short and our country will be deprived of the necessary means to help those who cannot contribute, wholly or partially, to the endeavours of the working population.
Now the government's white paper lays particular emphasis on the considerable number of income security programs which are based at present on a continuous improvement of economic growth during the last 50 years.
Our objectives are twofold: first a guaranteed income, and then the maintenance of income.
The guaranteed income reduces insecurity, temporarily alleviates financial difficulties and prevents or decreases poverty for most citizens who may expect to be part of the active population.
On the other hand, the maintenance of income is intended more directly for poor people because they cannot be part of the active population for various reasons beyond their will.
The white paper studies priorities in the light of modern problems. One of these is the existence of several important groups of people who lack resources and opportunities compared with most of their fellow citizens. Among these we find, naturally, the aged, who were discussed today, female heads of families with dependent children, the disabled and the working poor. I must say that the situation is particularly serious for female heads of families.
Now, simultaneously, some income protection programs are being increasingly criticized because they are universal. Still, they benefit all Canadians regardless of income and, in some cases, considerable amounts of money are paid to people of amply sufficient means.
Mr. Speaker, here is the challenge the government must now meet in its program: it must formulate a new income security policy that would allow assistance to those in greatest need of it, while respecting what other programs

March 23, 1972
Pension Increases
are intended to stimulate the economic development on which our present social welfare system is based.
Mr. Speaker, we must now concentrate our efforts on the fight against poverty. All hon. members will surely agree with me that this must be done in such a way as to allow the greatest possible concentration of available resources in aid to those whose income is the lowest. In every possible instance, selective payments, based on income, must be substituted for universal payments which do not take into account the real income of the recipient.
Moreover, social insurance programs should be extended to areas of prevention or reduction of poverty. The result should therefore be a more stable income basis for families and individuals, and in particular for older people with low income.
Government research on the ways to reach the objectives of this new policy has been very complete and has taken into consideration the opinions and the views of various groups, especially the criticism against existing programs.
The arguments in favour of a single guaranteed income system that would replace all existing income security programs have been studied in depth. Very few programs now carried out can be eliminated without causing grave prejudices to a number of people. The old age security pensions as well as the veterans pensions cannot be put aside at present. Furthermore, we think that a complete plan with adequate payments would be extremely burdensome. Nevertheless in the white paper the Canadian government has made proposals to extend a selective form of guaranteed income.
In our opinion the best way to offset the drawbacks of the existing system is not to replace our programs by a comprehensive guaranteed income plan, as some opposition members have suggested. It seems to us that the best way to do this is to review the guidelines for income security, to reassess the priorities and the scope of our plans and to find a kind of plan which will best enable us to achieve our main goals.
Our century, Mr. Speaker, has rapidly become the century dedicated to the well-being of the individuals. And it seems curious to me that today, through the motion that has been introduced, members opposite pretend not to realize that the government is bringing the utmost attention to this.
For the past ten years, in fact, the federal and the provincial governments have implemented a whole set of welfare measures to ensure a minimum of security for Canadians and for older citizens in particular.
The progress made indicates a real revolution in comparison with the previous situation. Let us remember the darker days of the economic crisis of 1927, when citizens had to fight alone to secure their daily subsistence.
It used to be that you had to ensure your security and subsistence for your old age. Now, governments take care of that for the citizens.
Programs such as medicare, hospitalization insurance and unemployment insurance protect the citizens against

the prohibitive costs of illness or loss of a job. Other programs including family allowances, social welfare, old age security pension and its supplement, aim at guaranteeing income security.
The best part of these social measures is borne by the federal government which earmarks one quarter of its yearly estimates for social security; in other words, 25 cents of every tax dollar is allocated to social security.
Welfare programs have been so expanded and diversified that they require constant updating and adaptation to modern changes. Indeed, the hon. members who moved this motion today intended to question some of our measures. I do not blame them for that, but I think it is strange that they do not take the opportunity of pointing out what the present government is doing precisely to help our senior citizens and those who are most underprivileged in Canada.
The federal government's white paper in particular made a great deal of the fact that we have to fight poverty. It is in this spirit that the government implemented its welfare measures. It is really inacceptable that in a society as affluent as ours, compared with several other countries of the world, there should still be people who lack the basic necessities.
No government is working with more energy toward eradicating social injustice and inequality in Canada than the government led by our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). The just society is not only a slogan. It is made more and more real everyday to the benefit of large families, elderly people and invalids.
Canada, which is recognized as having probably the best welfare system in the world, constantly tries to keep abreast of social progress.
I can say that from the cradle to the grave, the Canadian citizen can reckon on government's assistance to provide him with financial security.
And I do not think any class of society matters more in the eyes of the present government than those people who have to leave the mainstream of active life when they reach retirement age. More than anyone else, those people are entitled to a modicum of comfort and security.
Since today's world is centered on youth, it is often difficult to integrate the aged into the modern community. Though we must assist the young generation, we should not for all that neglect those who, through their work and devotion, have contributed to build the present.
Through the old age security plan, every senior citizen is entitled to a basic pension of $80 a month. Over the past few years, this plan has undergone major changes. The age of eligibility for a pension has been gradually reduced by the government from 70 to 65. Basic benefits have gone from $75 to $80 a month.
However, knowing that this income would not be sufficient for the needs of the elderly, considering the rise in the cost of living, the Canadian government initiated another old age security plan, the guaranteed income supplement. Added to the initial pension, and subject to a means test, this supplementary pension, which amounted originally to $31.83 a month for single persons and $63.66
March 23, 1972

for aged couples, has increased to $55 and $65 respectively.
These changes now enable a pensioner to draw a minimum monthly income of $135 instead of $113.61.
At the present time, 1,750,000 citizens receive a basic monthly pension of $80. It is estimated that some 470,000 individuals will draw the full amount of the guaranteed income supplement and that 550,000 others will receive partial benefits. This means that about 60 per cent of people over 65 will benefit from that program.
I think I should point out, Mr. Speaker, that at the present time the recipients of the old age pension alone or of the old age pension combined with the guaranteed income supplement already obtain tremendous assistance from the Canadian government. Their minimum income will be greatly increased when they begin to receive benefits under the Quebec or the Canada pension plan.
I would like to say in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that one million aged couples are directly receiving a guaranteed annual income of $3,060 from the federal government. It can be considered as a minimum protection but is undoubtedly a complete reversal of the conditions a few years ago. I believe that we can look to the future with optimism because, as retired persons will be receiving benefits under their pension plan and the government will be continuing to improve its pension plan, our senior citizens will certainly be drawing better incomes as they deserve.

Mr. Speaker, I can understand the minister's desire to cut short my speech, because in the 15 minutes at my disposal what I say will not necessarily be complimentary of the government.
I was speaking of the necessity of raising the old age pension for our senior citizens. I point out that this has nothing to do, I hope, with party politics. The question is whether our senior citizens are entitled not only to the gratitude of the Canadian people but to be paid the money which they have already put into the fund. I think the point has been clearly established that in fact we are not giving them anything; we are merely custodians of a very large fund which has been put aside to look after them in their old age. They are entitled to this money and I suggest that now is a good time to give them that to which they are fully entitled.
Not only old age pensioners are referred to in this motion; there is also the question of federal government pensions. I am affected personally in this regard and hope I will be allowed to comment on the subject. There is no fairness, and there never has been, in the way federal government pensions are handled. Anyone who has served the federal government, and through it the people of Canada, should have equitable treatment. If I had time to go into cases I would explain my own case.
Hon. members might be surprised to know that one could work in the civil service during peacetime, take a job during wartime, for example in the mounted police so that one was not subject to military service, go back to the civil service after the war, and all this service would count for pension purposes. However, in my case and in the case of several others this was not the situation. The lobby on this matter is very small and I have hesitated to raise it. I do so now because it is well worth looking into. I should like to know when this question will be considered without the necessity of lobbying.
Four, five or six people are affected in this manner. When you ask the government to look into these matters they say it is impossible to go back beyond a certain date; if your pension has not been calculated to a certain date it is impossible to go back beyond that date. I do not think that is justifiable. I think it is unfair. Adjustments have been made in respect of pensions, but what kind of adjust-

March 23, 1972
Pension Increases
merits? Pensions are usually adjusted on a percentage basis; therefore, if you are receiving $10,000 and there is a 10 per cent increase, you will receive an extra $1,000 a year. But if your pension is $40 a month, you get an increase of $4 a month which certainly does not lift you above the poverty level.
This kind of thing is unfair. This is not a question of petty politics at all. I am asking for equity and I hope that all parties in the House and all governments are interested in seeing that there is equity. It is no excuse for a government to say that equity cannot be given. Of course it can, and this House has the power to give it. If this House knows that inequitable treatment is given to civil servants, members of the mounted police or members of the armed forces, it is not only right but it is our duty to see that the inequity is eliminated. I should like to see justice done in this respect-and not only because I am personally involved.
Perhaps I have been delinquent in not taking up the case of the four or five people who are not able to stand in the House and speak. I am privileged to speak for myself, but I am not doing only that: I am begging that these matters be considered. They are well known to the authorities, to the civil service and to the mounted police. It is well known in every corner of Canada that people unfortunate enough to have retired 20 or 30 years ago receive a miserable pension which means they are living well below the poverty level. They are not in a position to come here and beg. I think it is my duty to raise this question. We have an army of civil servants in this country numbering hundreds of thousands. They should be interested. I beg them to look into this matter and bring forward recommendations so that these inequities can be corrected.
A few days ago we heard in the House about the magnificent treatment we are giving our veterans. I am happy at the steps that have been taken so far but I remind the House that it took us 26 years to do something for the Hong Kong veterans. Again, I take a personal interest in the Hong Kong veterans because I was there when the Winnipeg Grenadiers arrived in Winnipeg on their return from Hong Kong. I have sat in the veterans affairs committee and heard people ask what proof we have that these veterans are sick-because they have no wounds, no bullet holes! I carried off that train men who weighed 85 pounds and who when they joined the army weighed 185 pounds. What more proof do you need?
It took us 26 years to give them equity. It is suggested that we should be satisfied because we made it possible for them to receive a 50 per cent pension. I do not think we should be particularly proud of that, not after 26 years. It should be a 100 per cent pension for everyone who wants it, and certainly for everyone who needs it. These men have made heroic efforts to remain fully employed. Those boys who came back from Hong Kong were carried off in our arms, like babies, some of them blind. They made a wonderful recovery and I venture to say that for a great many of them the record is magnificent. They have gone back to Canadian public life, to the firms for which they worked, to the woods and to their farms, and to the best of their ability they have been 100 per cent productive. But they have done it with broken bodies.

It turns my stomach to hear anyone in the House or in the media say we have done a magnificent job of rewarding these people. I heard one hon. member here-I will not mention his name-point out that some of these fellows are getting $13,700 a year. That is a lie. He took the worst cases, people who are paraplegic, blind and without hope, added together the cost of their hospitalization and the miserable pittance their wives are receiving-wives who have spent 26 years nursing these hulks of humanity-and said we gave them $13,700 a year. This is about half what we get. And we call it magnificent! I do not want to call it a disgrace, and I know there is a bottom to the public purse-

Mr. Speaker, before six o'clock I was speaking about the Hong Kong veterans and the need that many of these men still have in spite of recent improvements to veterans legislation. In 1971 we in the veterans affairs committee were satisfied that we had finally given the old section 70, the benefit of the doubt provision, a new look. We have been assured that the benefit of the doubt will in fact be given to veterans. I am not at all worried about veterans abusing this section, particularly the Hong Kong boys who have done all they can for themselves. I believe the next move is up to us. Having got them to the 50 per cent level, it is up to us to consider the possibility of their needing a 100 per cent pension.
Over the years the compensation given to soldiers has been the same. The bench-mark has been the wage level of a labourer. We have never taken into account the special skills that a man had. Take the case of a professional pianist. He is not compensated at the level of his ability to play the piano. If he loses a hand, or both hands, he is compensated strictly at the labouring level. In the year 1972 we are still paying our veterans at the labouring level, but in effect we are not paying the full average wage of a labourer in Canada. I suggest that the level is now $5,000 or $6,000, the wage that is paid to the ordinary manual labourer, the cleaner on the Hill, the person who works with his muscles.
I know the taxpayer's pocket is not bottomless but I think we should live up to the agreement we intended to carry out in the first place, namely, to compensate our veterans according to their physical disability. If only that principle were followed I am sure the present level of veterans pensions would be shown to be far below the level of that which should be expected of a generous country such as ours. I do not want to draw comparisons with other countries, but I believe we are capable of giving our veterans a higher level of compensation. One may ask where we will get the money. It is a question of priority. I cannot think of a higher priority than paying
March 23, 1972

adequate pensions to the people who defended our country and enabled us for the past 25 or 26 years to enjoy the second highest standard of living in the world.
Many veterans become unemployable as they get on in years. They are incapable of maintaining themselves at a reasonable level of health. This is where section 70 should apply, particularly in respect of prisoners of war and men who have psychosomatic problems. As a modern nation we realize that psychosomatic problems can be just as damaging as physical wounds caused by gunshot.
We have made great strides in improving veterans legislation. I am proud of the strides we have made but I do not think we can sit back and say we have done all we can. Until we use the benefit of the doubt rule completely and take the soldier's word that he is suffering because of what happened to him during war, we cannot be completely fair. From personal experience I know that the best soldiers very rarely went sick. They do not have documents to prove every time they were sick. Most of the time they never went sick even if they had pneumonia or flu. I have seen in the front line men covered with boils, a very terrible and dangerous condition which can lead to complications. These men stayed in the front line and fought. They should have been hospitalized, but they would not leave their buddies. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having been advised of what many members of the opposition had to say about pensions this afternoon, I thought it would be helpful if I dealt with the policy considerations underlying the proposals already adopted by the government and the proposals that we have formulated for the future approval of this House. When I read what many members of the opposition have to say about pensions and how they would treat them, there seems to be a continuing determination not to resolve the philosophy that they ultimately wish to adopt in this whole area. I am referring, of course, to their remarks with regard to the guaranteed annual income while at the same time talking about increasing universal payments to everyone irrespective of income. In its simplest terms, this seems to me to point up a contradiction and a failure to come to grips with the policy that can best be adopted to help those in need of assistance.
As many hon. members know, the reasoning behind our income security proposals to date has been based on three techniques designed to assist people, to provide for their security and to prevent them from living in circumstances of deprivation. First, of course, is our social insurance scheme. I am referring particularly, in the income security context of pensions today, to the Canada Pension Plan. This is contributed to by people in the work force for protection upon their retirement as well as the premature death of the breadwinner. We have orphan benefits and survivor benefits of this kind. These programs assure Canadians of additional protection.
Pension Increases
I do not think anyone would argue that no matter what technique we move to in the future, whether it be toward the guaranteed annual income or the annual income technique such as in the guaranteed income supplement, we will always require social insurance schemes like the Canada Pension Plan. This plan provides protection for those in the work force who are earning wages which mean they are well above the poverty level, but they must have the protection that in the unfortunate eventuality of the premature death of the breadwinner or the retirement of the wage earner they will not have to use up all their savings and then fall into poverty. They will always have this protection. Whether we have a guaranteed income or anything else for those in the lower income group, we will always require the Canada Pension Plan. Therefore I think we can safely put that policy on the shelf in terms of any tinkering around with it, but certainly we should consider improving it and recognize the necessity that it be continued.
The next technique we have for income security is the demogrant, the universal payment that we all know-the old age security, the $80 a month that many members of the opposition have spoken of today, and family allowances. The third technique we have in terms of dealing with income maintenance and income support programs is to combine these programs with social services. We are doing that under the Canada Assistance Plan. These are the three main elements. There is the social insurance that we have had in the past and will need in the future, the demogrant of old age security and FISP, and then social services.
I should like to deal with demogrants. As a government, we have obviously decided that in terms of bringing money to those who need it in waging a successful campaign against poverty we must change from making universal payments to everyone, irrespective of income, to a selective technique. We must have an income test-I call it a guaranteed income technique-applied to what was previously our universal demogrant program of old age security and family allowance. We are doing that now and we have done it with respect to our aged with some very beneficial results. These are the three main areas. Social insurance we are going to improve, demogrants we are changing to a more selective technique to get more hundreds of millions of dollars to those who need it, and a strengthening of services to those in need, under the Canada Assistance Plan.
Before getting down to specifics about what we are doing in each of these categories I should like to refer to the NDP position relative to pensions for our senior citizens. If I am correct, this afternoon the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) referred to the universal aspect of this question. Perhaps the New Democratic Party will have an opportunity to reply later this evening. However, it would seem that the hon. member would do away with the guaranteed income supplement as a technique to deal with our senior citizens. He would seem to say that we should follow the old age security route, the $80 a month that is paid to each of our senior citizens, and increase that to $150 a month applied across the board to some 1,700,000 Canadians. No matter whether they were in destitute circumstances or were millionaires, they would each get $150 a month.

March 23, 1972
Pension Increases
When you start making universal payments to everybody, for each $10 increase in old age security it costs an additional $200 million per year; that is, raising it from $80 to $90 adds $200 million, from $80 to $100 adds $400 million, and so on. It is easy to figure out what it would cost in one year to raise the old age security from $80 a month to $150 a month for everyone in this country who is entitled to it. If we brought in the necessary measures in terms of taxing people in order to obtain that additional revenue-we would presumably have to tax to get it because we are already running a deficit, as opposition members constantly remind us-what would be the position of hon. members opposite? Would they favour, in one fell swoop for this category of persons, an allocation of upward of $11 billion in one year, fully realizing that there are in this country many people other than our senior citizens who are in dire need? That does not seem to be a practical approach, especially since many people who argue that we should make universal payments talk at the same time about the guaranteed annual income.
I know that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) did not specifically refer to this in his speech this afternoon; I do not think he got around to the guaranteed annual income. Nevertheless, many people argue, in favour of universal payments being made regardless of income-and of course when you talk about $150 a month you are talking about an attractive package-and argue at the same time in favour of a guaranteed annual income. I ask, what do they mean when they talk about a guaranteed annual income in this country? That is a technique that one uses in order to bring into play the principle of selectivity so that you provide resources to those most in need. In essence, that is what the guaranteed income is, and in that case you apply an income test. You can arrive at it through a negative income tax or you can pay it out universally and get back what you have overpaid through the tax system, or you can apply an income test before the income is paid out, which in essence is what we do with the guaranteed income supplement.
Whichever way you go about it, and disregarding for a moment what you mean when you talk about a guaranteed annual income, there is no doubt at all that you will do this through a selective method because you will also determine in some way how to provide resources to people who need them most. So there is a blatant contradiction in the argument of people who advocate universal payments on the one hand and the guaranteed annual income on the other. I think such people should be forced to reconcile their positions. Which road do they want to travel?
I would seriously argue, and I do not think anyone who thinks about this will disagree with me, that we just do not have the resources to adopt the universal technique and cope adequately with poverty in this country. The white paper on income security that I brought out some time ago indicated that if we were to adopt the guaranteed annual income technique for all Canadians and provide them with an income even at the poverty levels recommended by the Economic Council, the cost would be
(Mr. Munro.]
between $1.5 billion and $2.5 billion over and above what we are now spending.
Furthermore, roughly 30 per cent of the federal budget at present is being spent in this entire field. I point that out and ask those who talk in terms of universal payments and guaranteed annual income to come to grips with facts, because how can one reconcile the positions they have taken? Would they, for instance, recommend that upward of $1.5 billion of additional funds be spent on senior citizens and recommend as well that between $1.5 billion and $2.5 billion be applied to other Canadians who need assistance? It seems to me that we are talking about staggering amounts of money.
One must remember, also, that the government is faced with criticism emanating from the Economic Council, various commissions and Senate committees which have gone into the question of poverty. Time after time we hear it said that a very great part of our resources is going into our income security system but that the money is not reaching those who need it most. People talk in terms of universal payments without at the same time explaining where we are to get the money. They talk about universal payments without at the same time indicating how they are prepared to reconcile that position with the guaranteed income technique.
Having said that, I should like to say that in this whole area, and especially in the area of the senior citizen, the government's record is one of which we can be justly proud. In 1957 the old age security pension was $56 a month. The Diefenbaker administration took over in 1957. That administration lasted to 1963. It raised the $56 to $65 per month. That represented an increase of $9 over a period of about six years.
When the Liberal government took over in 1963 the pension was $65 per month payable at age 70. We increased that amount considerably and brought in the guaranteed income supplement. In 1966 we introduced into the system an additional $30 per month through the guaranteed income supplement and brought in for the first time-no government up to that time had done this- the cost of living escalator of 2 per cent a year which was to be paid on top of the pension. Approximately one year ago we brought in the second biggest increase in the history of Canada in the guaranteed income supplement. We brought that $105 figure up to $135 for a single person and up to $255 per month for married senior citizens over the age of 65.
I might add that during this whole period we gradually lowered the eligible age from 70 to 65. I am advised, and I concur in this advice having done some research into income security systems for senior citizens in all other countries of the free world, that no plan of any country in the free world provides the protection for senior citizens that our plan provides for our senior citizens.

I have not referred to the strengthening of services that we provide for our senior citizens through the Canada Assistance Plan. Many hon. members may be aware that under cost-sharing arrangement whereby we share 50-50 with provinces the costs of certain services we also share costs with respect to the provision of many
March 23, 1972

ancillary services for our senior citizens. Some of the provinces are providing drugs for our senior citizens, especially those on GIS. We are paying half those costs.
Many social and rehabilitative agencies throughout the country have been set up to help our senior citizens and we share in the cost of that service. We help in that area, to say nothing of the help we provide with hospitalization and medical care coverage. In that area we pay roughly 50 per cent of the cost to the provinces. Many of our senior citizens who are on GIS are supplied by certain provinces with hospitalization cards, with no premium required. I am talking about the provinces which cover their half of the costs through collecting premiums. As I say, we pay for half of these services. All these supplementary services are being made available to our senior citizens. I do not think any country does better than Canada in terms of assisting senior citizens. I have not mentioned the many millions of dollars-and these expenditures are increasing each year-spent on housing through Central Mortgage and Housing. In that way we are providing homes for our senior citizens throughout this country.
So when you look at the whole complex of policies designed to assist our senior citizens, I think the Canadian government and the people of Canada can justifiably be proud. We have evolved policies; we have shown originality in that field. Although we are spending in excess of $2 billion a year on our senior citizens, the money is well spent. Our older people are guaranteed a minimum income floor, and supplementary services made available through the Canada Assistance Plan are improving each year.
I also want to talk about the escalator aspect. When we gave all those receiving the guaranteed income supplement the right to an automatic 2 per cent escalation in pension payments, we achieved a breakthrough. Some members of the opposition thought so too. When people talk about people receiving $80 a month they are talking about those who receive only the old age security pension. If somebody receiving the old age security also qualifies for all or part of the guaranteed income supplement, the 2 per cent escalation applies to the whole amount, to the OAS portion as well as to the guaranteed income supplement portion. Approximately two-thirds or our senior citizens are receiving all or part of the guaranteed income supplement, thus two-thirds of them are receiving the 2 per cent escalation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over the years the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) has sat in this House I have developed considerable affection for him. But that will not cause me to be diverted from the subject before us this evening. I listened to the minister bring forward a long series of red herrings such as the universal approach to old age pensions, the guaranteed annual income and various other benefits. However, none of these is the subject of this debate. The resolution which we are discussing reads as follows:
That this House condemns the government's failure to contribute to pensions, allowances and other benefits granted or administered by the government a yearly percentage increase corresponding to the percentage increase in the consumer price index for Canada.
What is referred to in the resolution is a very important and basic principle. When a government makes a commitment to individuals, that commitment should be honoured in the real value in which it was made and should not be discharged in debased coinage. That is what happens in a period of inflation. If you think about it for even a few moments you will realize that almost all government commitments are made in terms of absolute dollars. The result is that a commitment to pay a pension at any level, or any other commitment that is stated in dollars, has a decreasing value as inflation decreases the value of the dollar. Although the government may be adhering to the letter of its own law, it is not adhering to the spirit of the law.
The results in a period of inflation are as follows. Not only are the government's commitments to individuals almost invariably measured in an absolute number of dollars, but government receipts or expected receipts are almost always calculated in terms of percentage of income. What is the result of this? On the government's receipts side of the ledger, a period of inflation has the effect that basic exemptions in taxation are measured in absolute dollars. As inflation continues, the real value of those exemptions goes down, so that in terms of real value the tax burden imposed on individuals or corporations increases in absolute purchasing power without the legislation being changed at all. The government's take of the gross national product automatically increases.
On the other side of the ledger, the paying out side, the government discharges its commitments in what is in effect debased coinage at a much lower real value than that which existed when the commitment was made. The government benefits from this in a bookkeeping way because in a period of inflation the government's tax receipts go up but its commitments to pay out do not go up in the same proportion. It is in a position of affluence, so to speak.
The trouble with governments over the years, particularly this one and perhaps even more the previous one, has been that in a period of inflation or what may be called buoyancy they are well off as far as receipts are concerned. With regard to what they have to pay out, they become prodigal. They think of setting up more boards and studies and hiring more and more civil servants who are put to work at jobs that are ever decreasing in importance and benefit ratio to cost as far as the country as a whole is concerned. In those periods the overhead to be borne by government increases at a tremendous rate.

Then we encounter a period in which this trend disappears; the government is hard up and is forced to run a deficit to stimulate the economy. Surely this is a time when we ought to do our national business in a more scientific manner.
In present circumstances, every government has a vested interest in inflation for the reasons I have stated. If the value of the dollar decreases, it can discharge its obligations in cheap money. Surely this is wrong in principle. I am reminded of the story told about a medieval weaver who had a lot of cloth to sell. In those days the measure of a yard was the distance between the king's nose and his thumb when the arm was extended. It so happened that the heir apparent was a runt, so the weaver tried to kill the king in order that he could settle his obligations in short yards of cloth. This is the way in which this government and governments before it have operated. I think we ought to do better than that.
The resolution suggests, therefore, that when a government enters upon an obligation it should discharge that obligation in terms of the real value at the time it was made, and not in cheap dollars. The present practice of governments making commitments prior to a period of inflation and then discharging them as inflation decreases the value of the dollar is really an example of Indian-giv-ing. The administration brags about the goodies it handed out and soon afterward people find that the value of those goodies has shrunk to 80 per cent of what it was originally. The administration then brings it back to perhaps 90 per cent of the original value and then brags about its performance again.
Who suffers when the government pays off its obligations in cheap money? One such group includes the aged, because a lot of the aged are poor. The aged in Canada account for an appallingly large proportion of the poor. Thirty-two per cent of all families whose heads are aged between 65 and 69 are poor. Forty-nine per cent of all unattached individuals aged between 65 and 69 are poor. Sixty-seven per cent of all unattached individuals over the age of 70 are poor. These figures for 1969 are supplied by Statistics Canada.
Another group which suffers in these circumstances includes the veterans of our country. In 1919, when the basic value in real terms of veterans pensions was set, it was decided that it should be the equivalent of the wages of an unskilled worker in the civil service. Recently, members of our armed forces received a deserved raise in pay. Their pay was brought up to parity with that of the civil service. The pay of a private soldier was increased, retroactive to October 1, 1971, to $5,760 per year. Mr. Speaker, the basic rate of pension for a single pensioner is only $3,504. The differential is $2,256.
The Woods committee on veterans pensions recommended that the amount fixed for a 100 per cent pension should continue to be directly related to the earning power of a man in the class of an untrained labourer as determined by the average wage for this type of employment in the public service. The Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs approved this recommendation in its report to the House of Commons on June 22, 1970. A
March 23, 1972

sampling of public service pay scales indicates that the average basic pay of such employees as of October, 1971, was $4,551. So the basic pay of a veteran has fallen away behind this figure. I believe it is $3,504 at the present time.
This is a further illustration of the erosion over the years, due to a decrease in the value of the dollar, of a basic value which was established originally. When the disparity is made up, it is never made up entirely. In any case the adjustment is always made late and the value of the new scale begins to decrease almost immediately. Bearing these points in mind, I have great pleasure in supporting the motion criticizing the government for failing to recognize the principle, which is justice, nothing more.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to take part in this debate, even briefly. I do not think anyone in this chamber is unaffected by the appeals we receive through the mail and personally from our constituents and others who live in this wonderful land but who are not sufficiently endowed with its worldly goods.
Responsibility for dividing the wealth of the nation rests upon the government, particularly with respect to the wealth which accrues to the treasury through taxation. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) has this evening presented to us the case for the government. The division he has outlined is a sensible one and one I can support-a division of resources between various programs which are directed mainly to those who are in greatest need. This, however, is but one point of view, I would suggest. I believe there are others which would bear investigation and I intend to come to them in a few moments. Before doing so I should like to refer to comments of previous speakers concerning veterans in general and Hong Kong veterans in particular.
In the case of Hong Kong veterans, Mr. Speaker, you will recall it was only a matter of a few months ago that this House agreed that the Hong Kong veterans were to be given special treatment in view of their disabilities and the treatment they suffered while prisoners of war. They have now been awarded a sufficiently large percentage of pension to ensure that their widows are given protection when they pass on. The widows of their comrades who have already passed on are, I believe, now better looked after than they were before. I think this has been a very great achievement which was not the result of the efforts of any one member of the House but of general agreement among all members of the veterans affairs committee. I think this has been a real step forward.
I was also pleased to receive in the mail this evening additional evidence of another step forward taken by the veterans affairs committee in the form of the decision in the first appeal presented to the Pension Appeals Board recently set up by the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Laing). I am glad to say we are now seeing how the benefit of the doubt clause is being applied to those for whom it was designed.
As mentioned earlier by my hon. friend opposite, too many veterans are inadequately documented. Possibly the
Pension Increases
worst documented group, as I have told the House previously, are the veterans who served overseas. The best documented veteran in the world is the man who did not leave Canada or get far from his Canadian base. Therefore, my sympathies lie entirely with the badly documented veteran who saw service overseas, and I am very pleased that he now has the benefit of the additional protection that has been given him by this parliament. I think this has been another very great step forward taken by the House.
I should now like to come back to a final matter in connection with veterans affairs before I pass on, in the very few moments I have left, to the question of pensions generally. I wish to bring to the attention of the Minister of Veterans Affairs as forcefully as I can-I think this lies within the ambit of this debate-the fact that domiciliary care for veterans is very much a federal problem. If provinces choose not to provide domiciliary care facilities for their older citizens, certainly for veterans, then I think this government-indeed, any government-as well as this House and the country have a responsibility to provide them. Recognizing this, I hope it will be one of the steps the new Minister of Veterans Affairs will take during his term of office. I also hope it will be one of the matters to which the veterans affairs committee will apply itself very diligently in the weeks ahead.
The matter is becoming a very pressing one. Veterans of the Second World War are requiring domiciliary care. They cannot get it from the provincial establishments and they cannot afford to obtain it privately. So where are they to go? That is a question which at the moment is unanswered and it can only be answered by this House.
In conclusion I wish to speak about pensions generally. I think we are all receiving letters from our constituents who find it a problem to make ends meet in these days of inflation. I should like to read one of these letters to the House. It arrived today and is written by someone who lives in Victoria whom I will not name. He writes:
-I wish to draw your attention to the situation of retired civil servants who are restricted to an annual pension increase of only 2 per cent at a time when those presently employed are being awarded 7 per cent, 8 per cent and even more each year.
If MPs. can claim $8,000 per year, and if employed personnel can prove a need for increases on their present high salaries, surely the need is much more obvious for those of us who reached retirement age when salaries were much lower.
The following is the most moving, Mr. Speaker:
As the present trend continues, each year reduces our standard of living and makes the prospect of growing old rather terrifying, which is hard to understand in this richly endowed land of ours.
If nothing better can be done, surely our Pensions should at least be tied onto a cost of living bonus, or failing this an increase in the old age pension somewhat better than 42 cents.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say, first of all, I was very much impressed by the speech of the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Groos). I only wish the exigencies of our parliamentary procedure would enable him to put his vote where his convictions obviously lie, that is, in favour of the motion and the amendment, because I believe he made a most eloquent and moving plea for precisely what is in those documents. I shall not blame him if he yields to the general practice in this place of voting according to party, but certainly his remarks would be even more impressive if he joined those

who support the motion and the amendment because they are clearly in line with what he said.
I did not have the opportunity to hear the whole of the speech of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro), but I heard enough of it to note the tone of extreme complacency about the record of the government in this field. The minister said that he thinks the Canadian government has reason to be proud of what it has done for the old age pensioners. He said that the Canadian people have reason to be proud. I note that the minister is not in the House now, but perhaps he will read the record of this debate. I wish to give him some news. The government may be proud, but the people of Canada are not proud of the record in respect of what we have been able to do for our old age pensioners. They are disappointed. In fact, I am prepared to assert that nothing else the government has done or has failed to do has created more disillusionment in this country than its treatment of the old age pensioners.
I took the trouble to make a survey of opinion in my riding. I asked two questions which are relevant to this debate. A number of other questions were asked as well. I asked whether government old age pensions and old age assistance are to low. This is a very simple question. There were 562 answers to the question. There were 514 affirmative answers and 48 negative answers. So out of a sampling of nearly 600, the number of persons who believe old age pensions are too low is in the ratio of five to one. Then I thought that perhaps the people who answered this question might be interested because they themselves might be recipients of old age security or assistance. I asked if that was the case, and it turned out that only 90 persons were in that group and 411 were not.
If this sampling of opinion is sound, and I believe it is, I say that the vast majority of the Canadian people wish us to do more for our old age pensioners. Then I asked another question. These questions were under a number of headings. I asked: "How do you rate the performance of the federal Trudeau government in the following areas". The three choices I gave were "very good," "satisfactory" and "poor." Then I listed each area of performance of the federal government. In the area of security for senior citizens, 33 answered "very good", 158 answered "satisfactory" and 342 said "poor". I might say that some included other adjectives; some said "lousy" and some said "disgraceful". They expressed themselves very clearly in that way although they were not asked to do so in the questionnaire.
This sampling in my own constituency indicated that the performance of the government in that field has been poor. I suggest that the minister, instead of basking in the sort of complacency he exhibited today, should seek the opinion of his constituents and find out whether the performance of the government in this field is as good as he made it out to be.
I would have been perfectly content so far as this debate is concerned to have said that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) expressed, as he has on a number of other occasions, precisely, eloquently and clearly the position I take on behalf of my constituents in respect of the old age pension and other forms of security. But, and I recognize that what I say may be purely repeti-
March 23, 1972

tive, there are too many in my constituency who are deeply and personally concerned with this matter to make it adequate for me to say merely that I repeat and accept the views of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, although I do wholeheartedly accept those views. There are too many people in my constituency who have worked hard all their lives, who have struggled to build their homes, who have struggled to bring up their families, who have contributed to this country and who find under the present situation that they are strained, that they are pressured, and in some cases are even starved because of the situation in which they now find themselves.
I should like to say I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in what I understood him to say, that is, we in this party believe a very minimum that should be done at this time is that which is set out in the motion we are debating. That motion asks that all pensions include an escalator clause corresponding to the increase in the cost of living. I would say that is indeed the very minimum we could ask for. Every time the cost of living increases and the escalator clause we have of 2 per cent does not equal the increasing cost of living, we are taking something away from the old age pensions that the Canadian people have promised to the older people of this country. We are depriving them of something to which, in my view, they are entitled. I do not think we should be satisfied with that sort of performance; I think it is inconsistent with the clear promises of the parliament, the party and the government which originally produced the plan, and it is unworthy of the Canadian people.
I accept the motion and I accept the amendment that has been moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. It deals with the failure of the government to raise to adequate levels the basic amount of all personal pensions, allowances and benefits. I share with my colleague surprise that the official opposition in its motion paid no heed to this particular problem. I share with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre the belief that an increase to $150 a month for a single person and $300 a month for a married couple is not one dollar too much. I believe this country can afford it. The minister said it represents a colossal figure and extra taxation at a time of deficit. I remind the minister and members of the House that for 500,000 people who are receiving the full supplement at the moment the increase is only from $135 to $150 per person.
I also repeat, because it bears repeating, that those
500,000	people, because the supplement is so small, arrive at a position of complete destitution. For another 500,000 there is an increase from an average of about $125 to $150, and only for 700,000 is there an increase from $80 to $150. It seems to me that this is not only justice, this is not only the carrying out of contractual moral obligations to our older people; it would be a fillip to the economy. The effect of this would be expansionary at a time when we need expansion, and where could expansion be more justly and properly devoted than to relieving the hardships of the older people of this country?
I think it was in 1970 that the government froze the pensions of some 500,000 old age pensioners who did not receive the guaranteed income supplement at $80 a
Pension Increases
month. This increased pensions at that level by 42 cents a month. The government has done very little else that has done more to discredit them with the people of this country than that increase of 42 cents a month. This increase did not even reflect the increase in the cost of living up to that time. As for the cost of living which has risen and will rise in the future, no increase has been or will be made in that amount.
I say that this is contrary to the principle of universality adopted in 1950. The contract of the government has been broken. The principle for old age pensions as adopted was that pensions should escalate with the cost of living. That legislation and its continuance constitutes, in my view, a breach of faith. Ministers of government such as Miss LaMarsh, then minister of national health and welfare, Mr. Pearson, then prime minister, and Mr. Benson, then minister of finance, have stated from time to time that all future old age pensions should automatically be increased according to the increase in the cost of living. This pledge to our older people has been broken. I urge that old age pensions are not a matter of charity but a matter of right. Payments into the old age pension fund are partly out of the general revenue, it is true, but much of the amount is raised by the pensioners themselves through income tax and sales tax.
When this legislation was introduced, and since that time, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated that the effect of the government's legislation was to take from the rich and pay to the poor. I suggest that that is not a fair description of what has happened. In fact, there has been a redistribution of poverty. Forty per cent of all those who receive the old age pension get no guaranteed income supplement and have no increase at all. Perhaps 10 per cent of them have substantial means but the other 30 per cent, amounting to half a million people, have incomes of between $3,500 and $4,000 a year. Are these the rich from whom more is to be taken in order to benefit the other people? I suggest that this is a complete mistake.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has repeated many times in the House that this party stands for a basic pension for all people over 65 years of $150 without any means or income test. We in this party do not propose to go back on that part of our policy. In fact, we wish to go forward and reduce the age at which old age pensions would be paid, thus distributing income at this time. I conclude by saying that we are anticipating an election fairly soon and I say to the government that they will be the ones to suffer if they allow the election to come on without changing their attitude, without adopting either the motion put forward by the official opposition or accepting the amendment of this party.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to say something about the motion put forward by the official opposition. What the motion means, of course, is very simple to everyone in the House of Commons tonight, namely, that all Canadians on pensions are not getting enough money, particularly our senior citizens who are commonly called old age pensioners and those who spent a long time in the army and are now entitled to the war veterans allowance.
Other hon. members who have taken part in the debate referred to those who are fortunate enough to be on the

March 23, 1972
Pension Increases
Canada Pension Plan, who receive widows allowances, family allowances, and so on. I do not think there is a single member in the House of Commons who would not agree that pensioners, whether they be old age pensioners, veteran pensioners or any other pensioners, should obtain more money. All of us accept that fact. When I look back over the years, and one does not have to go back too far, I realize that old age pensions in Canada were initiated on a means test at $20 a month. I remember when it was increased to $40 a month for pensioners who had reached the age of 70. That was within the last 25 years or thereabouts.
In those days our older people were the ones who, like our senior citizens of today, had helped to make Canada great. They were pleased and proud of the fact that what they had done in life was appreciated by the taxpayers of Canada and they were most happy to accept the $40 a month, which of course is a mere pittance when we think of what is being done today. I remember sitting in the Ontario legislature when the hon. Walter Harris sat on the government side as minister of finance in the House of Commons and on that budget night raised the old age pension given to persons at the age of 70 from $40 to $46 a month. I remember the sneers that greeted the statement of the minister of finance which were expressed in the press throughout Canada and by members of the opposition who said that he was simply not giving enough. On looking back, most people would agree with them.
What happened that members of the opposition, and indeed members of my own party, as my hon. friend to the left suggested, agreed that that was not enough? You may remember that we had an election. Our Conservative friends to the left-I certainly regard them as my friends-immediately raised the old age pension to the magnificent sum of $55 a month, and before they called another election they raised it to $65 a month for all Canadians, for the wealthy and the poor, at age 70. There were many of us-I was one of them and I am sure there are many such people on my side of the House-who agreed that it was nice to get a pension increase. It was a large sum, but let us look at the situation today. Hon. friends to my left are talking about a heaven; they are not talking about the old age pension as it is today or as it was yesterday. They have suggested that we have a heaven on earth but they have not suggested the figure that would be appropriate to the situation in Canada today.
I say with all sincerity, Mr. Speaker, that if the government of Canada offered the old age pensioners $200 a month, the very next day hon. members to my left would be up in the House of Commons asking for $250 a month.
